speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all hon. members were shocked as I was to learn of the death earlier today of one of our number, Mr. Gaspard Boucher, who represented the constituency of Restigouche-Mada-waska in this house.
Mr. Boucher was elected to the House of Commons for the first time on August 10, 1953, after a long and distinguished career in his native province of New Brunswick. A printer and publisher by profession, he was president of the Madawaska Printing Office and Bookstore Limited, and editor of the weekly newspaper Le Madawaska or The Madawaska, published in both languages. During his career as a newspaperman, he was always keenly devoted to the interests of the residents of his county and of his province.
In 1935 he was elected to the legislature of New Brunswick and was given renewed votes of confidence during the succeeding elections of 1939, 1944 and 1948. From 1936 to 1939 he served as deputy speaker of the legislature. From 1940 to 1949 he was chairman of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission and from 1949 to 1952 secretary-treasurer in the provincial government.
Although his career as a member of this parliament was regrettably brief, Mr. Boucher made a substantial contribution to several of the committees of this house. As was natural because of his background and experience in those fields, his views were very helpful to the committees on printing, public accounts, and banking and commerce. He was also an effective member of other committees, including that on railways, canals and telegraph lines and the committee on mines, forests and waters. Unfortunately, his failing health did not permit him to take the active part in our debates which he would have liked.
I feel confident that all members will join with me, Mr. Speaker, in expressing our sincere regret at the loss of a member whose knowledge and experience we all appreciated and in extending our sincere condolences to Mrs. Boucher and the other members of the family in their bereavement.
(Translation) :
Our friend Gaspard Boucher, who for many years was prominent in the field of public affairs, was also particularly devoted to the interests of the French-speaking citizens of his province. He will be remembered as a Canadian who faithfully and worthily represented his fellow citizens both in the New Brunswick legislature and in this house where, unfortunately, his failing health these past few years prevented him from being as active as he had been.
May we again extend to his wife and his family our deepest sympathy on the occasion of their bereavement.
(Text):

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with the Prime Minister and the other members of this house in expressing heartfelt sympathy to the widow and children of Mr. Boucher in the sad loss they have suffered. It does come home to us on an occasion of this kind that, with whatever political opinions we may seek to express our services in this house, there is a close and intimate association amongst the members, which finds very clear and deep expression at this time. Like so many of the other members in the house, Mr. Boucher was a man of wide and long experience, not only in the provincial legislature, but in the many local activities which contribute so much to the strength of the life of the whole nation. He was very active in those local enterprises which advance the health and strength and interest of young people, as well as in those social organizations which play their important part in the building of the character of every community. On an occasion like this it seems that it is extremely difficult to use words which in themselves convey to those who have been bereaved the sentiments we feel. I feel sure that in joining with the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and in extending to him and his colleagues our sympathy in their loss, we may also express the hope that for Mrs. Boucher and his children there will be some real measure of comfort in the knowledge that those who have been associated with him in the House of Commons are thinking of them at this time.

The late J. G. Boucher

Mr. Speaker, it was only just as I came into the building a few minutes ago that I learned the sad news of Mr. Boucher's passing. I want to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in expressing to Mrs. Boucher and her family our sympathy in their sorrow. I would also couple with that remark our sympathy to the Prime Minister and the members of the party with which Mr. Boucher was associated in the loss of a colleague.
I did not know Mr. Boucher well. He has been here, of course, for only a year and a half and in that time one does not get to know all of the members of the house. But from what I know of him-and I met him casually two or three times-I thought he was a fine gentleman who would have made a real contribution in this parliament had he been permitted to do so.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a matter of great regret when members of our association here in parliament pass on. Especially is that so when members with such broad experience as that of Mr. Boucher are called prematurely, it seems, into the next phase of existence. We join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in expressing sympathy to the wife and the family of Mr. Boucher. While I did not know Mr. Boucher too well, I was associated with him in the banking and commerce committee. If he had been privileged to live longer, I think he would have made a real contribution in this house, in view of his sincerity and the great background of experience that he had had in his native province of New Brunswick. We also express our sympathy to the Prime Minister and his party in the loss of a devoted follower.

Mr. Speaker, those who have spoken with reference to the passing of our good friend Gaspard Boucher have paid him a fine tribute; but on behalf of the Liberal members from the province of New Brunswick I should just like to add a few words. I have known Gaspard Boucher for about thirty years, and I can say that few men in the province of New Brunswick have given more of their life for the benefit of their fellow men than has Gaspard Boucher. He was a most valued member of our provincial legislature for many years. As has been said, he was deputy speaker. He was then chairman of the New Brunswick hydro commission. For the last few years he was a provincial member he was our provincial secretary treasurer. On behalf of the members from New Brunswick I should like to extend sincere sympathy to 
Mrs. Boucher and her family. We realize at this time that the counties and the province which he represented have lost a fine citizen.

As far as could be determined from thorough investigations by service police and, in some instances, civil police, R.C.M.P. and the chief auditor, 13 complaints were found to be without foundation; four of these complaints indicated a possible malicious intent. Investigation into an additional four complaints revealed that, in fact, these complaints were not warranted; two of them appear to have been made by eccentrics. One complaint received was not sufficiently specific to make an investigation possible.
With respect to the remaining four complaints of the 22 complaints in which investigations have been completed:

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STRIKE OF GRAIN HANDLERS AT LAKEHEAD
speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. What is being done to bring about an early settlement of the strike of lakehead grain handlers in order to prevent economic unsettlement and serious distress in the marketing of wheat and other farm products on the prairies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STRIKE OF GRAIN HANDLERS AT LAKEHEAD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) sent me notice this morning of a similar question, part of which corresponds with the question of the hon. member for Prince Albert. In view of the importance of this matter I would ask that I might have the opportunity to give a little of the background of this dispute, one that I assure you has been causing my department concern now for a good many months.
The last agreement which was in effect between local 650 of the brotherhood of railway and steamship clerks, freight handlers, express and station employees and the lake-head terminal elevators association, representing elevator companies at Fort William and Port Arthur, was for a period of one year, terminating December 31, 1953. Pursuant to the terms of the collective agreement, local 650 of the brotherhood gave notice to the association that it wished to revise the agreement increasing wage rates and improving working conditions. Following this notice, the

Inquiries of the Ministry negotiating committees of the association and the local carried out direct negotiations subsequent to the termination date, but little progress toward a settlement was made.
On March 24, 1954, the lakehead terminal elevators association requested me to appoint a conciliation officer to deal with matters in dispute between the parties. The department's senior conciliation officer in Winnipeg was appointed on March 29, 1954. On June 11 the conciliation officer reported that he was unable to effect a settlement of the dispute, and on June 21 I established a conciliation board to deal further with the dispute. The board was fully constituted on July 19, 1954, with His Honour Judge Dowler of Port Arthur as chairman.
The board directed its efforts towards getting the parties back into negotiations on the issues in dispute with the result that on December 16, 1954, it was able to report that the parties "had been successful in settling all the issues except wages." On this issue the brotherhood had requested that the base rate paid at the lakehead be increased to the level of the wage rate paid by Vancouver elevator companies, with an additional 10 cents per hour to compensate for the dust hazard. On December 16, 1954, I received the report of the conciliation board, signed by the chairman and the nominee of the brotherhood, recommending a general increase of 3 per cent for all classifications affected.
Following receipt by the parties of copies of the report of the board, which I conveyed to them, the brotherhood advised me that the board's recommendation was unacceptable. The association of employers, in view of the decision of the brotherhood, did not express any view on the board's recommendation. Subsequently, my department arranged a further meeting between representatives of the parties in Ottawa on February 15. Some progress was made and a further meeting was arranged for a later date at the lakehead. This meeting was held but adjourned without results. A further conference between the parties initiated by the Canadian vice president of the brotherhood was held at Fort William on March 29, but no further progress towards a settlement was made.
My department was subsequently informed that a strike vote would be taken and immediately on receipt of the result of such vote I appointed Mr. Eric Taylor of Toronto as mediator to confer with the parties and use his best efforts to bring them into agreement. Advice to this effect was conveyed to the parties on April 13.
There was some indication that a strike would not take place until the parties had

met with the mediator, and meetings with them were accordingly arranged by him to take place on Tuesday morning, April 19- that is tomorrow morning. When it was learned on Saturday, April 16, that the employees had initiated strike action, Mr. Taylor proceeded at once to the lakehead and is now actively engaged in efforts to resolve the dispute and obtain a resumption of operations.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: Has the Minister of National Defence any statement to make to the house concerning the disastrous fire at Rockcliffe airport?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FIRE AT ROCKCLIFFE BARRACKS
speechtext:
I believe the facts with reference to this very regrettable fire have been fairly well covered by the press, but I might add a few observations.
As everyone knows, the fire took place at midnight on April 16, in barracks block 73, which is a second world war barrack block building, accommodating about 100 airmen. The station fire department arrived at the scene of the fire approximately two minutes after it was discovered by an airman.
Within a very few minutes they were joined by firemen from the Ottawa city fire department. Apparently there was adequate equipment, and it operated satisfactorily. It was almost 2 a.m. when the fire was finally brought under control. There was heavy damage to the south end of the east wing, and the washroom corridor on the second floor. The remainder of the building suffered water and smoke damage.
The evacuation alarm was sounded by the airman who discovered the fire, and he immediately began rousing others from their sleep. Intense smoke and heat however prevented anyone from entering the south end of the east wing on the second floor where the fire had originated. Some airmen did escape from this area through the windows but, most regrettably, two young airmen were trapped and died in the fire. Nine others received minor injuries.
The cause of the fire is as yet undetermined. An investigation is now under way by the Royal Canadian Air Force, the R.C.M.P., the Ontario fire marshal's office and the Ottawa fire department.

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, March 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Marler
Railway Act
for the second reading of Bill No. 259, to amend the Railway Act.

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments moved by the Minister of Transport on the motion for second reading of the bill that he suggested would remove the impediments to the operation of the act are now well known to us. Probably they will work out the way the minister has suggested with regard to five of the six proposals he presented, but the fifth, which limits the fund to $7 million, if the amount of the uncommitted balance is over $2 million on April 1 of any year, instead of being cumulative, indicates that this is a continuation of the sloth that made the momentum in accomplishment so sluggish and has brought about the consequent dissatisfaction with the board's present policy. It seems that the policy is to be the same, and I say the whole question should be examined.
I should like to refer to the statement of the minister that the board did not initiate projects, and that it acts only upon the petition of interested parties. The board should be in a position to initiate, and should not always leave to others the decision as to whether a project is needed, because the financial positions of some municipalities are such that many urgently needed projects will never be built. The board should be in a position to act on its own to protect the public.
At the time the board made an examination of the whole project they did not have the power to deal with the problem of unemployment that confronted this house last year. The minister said that unemployment was not one of the problems that confronted the board at that time, which is right; but since it has been injected into this arena- I mentioned it in debate the other day-it is a very important matter at the present time, and if the board had had the information at that time probably it would have introduced it as a subject to assist in solving our unemployment problem.
When the unemployment problem was considered some ten years ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) suggested that shelves of work would be provided to take care of unemployment in the future, and that municipalities and provinces were to have shelves of work set aside for that purpose. That situation has now arrived. Such projects as grade separations and the protecting of crossings with safety devices are matters that lend themselves to consideration at this time. That was the reason why I introduced it in my remarks. I thought it would help to solve the problem of unemployment and would prevent grade crossing accidents, without making work just for the

Railway Act
sake of making work. This is a shelf of work that would lend itself to removing grade level crossing hazards and at the same time it would help to relieve unemployment next year.
It seems that tail these problems are discussed or considered when we are right in the middle of them and nothing can be done. When the dominion-provincial conference meets, this question should be put on the agenda. The only reason why it was not considered by the board of transport commissioners when they were studying the question was that they were not asked to consider it.
Some papers made mention of the fact that there was no necessity to go into the whole problem because accidents were happening in remote sections of the country and also Dn grade crossings that were protected at the present time; therefore you could not take care of the indifference of the people who were driving, if they could not keep themselves out of accidents. I am not disregarding that point. It is quite true. But if the attitude were taken by industry, whether construction or manufacturing, that because of the indifference of the people no attention should be given to preventing accidents, I am quite sure we would have an appalling situation in the country. Because people are indifferent to the protection provided for them in accident prevention devices and disregard them is no reason why we should not continue to examine this problem which is causing concern to the people of Canada.
I am interested not only in unemployment but in the matter of safety regulations on the highways. This question has been touched on by some speakers. It should also be on the agenda of the dominion-provincial conference and should be tied in not only with safety on the highways but with an over-all accident prevention program. The whole question of safety should be studied., and standard regulations on the highways should be adopted so that all the people from Nova Scotia to British Columbia would be familiar with them and the safety regulations would all be the same. Then when tourists come to this country they could readily adapt themselves to the safety practices, precautions and devices that have been established.
These are some of the points that I thought should have been emphasized when the minister made his remarks on his motion for second reading. The unemployment factor and the factor of placing a limitation of $7 million on the fund are very important. The limitation on the fund is going to get us back into the position we were in formerly,

and very little will be done. I am satisfied that while $5 million is a vast improvement, it will not take care of the situation that presents itself, nor will it solve our problems.

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I have a few comments to make because it seems to me that the principle of this bill is very important. There is a great job to be done in this country so far as the removal of level crossings is concerned not only from the standpoint of safety-because we all realize that there is a great toll in human lives each year from crossing accidents-but also from the standpoint of convenience. I know of many localities in Canada where the failure to provide for proper access from one side of a railway track to another has brought about serious inconvenience. I am thinking of my own constituency where on occasion traffic is held up for a considerable period of time owing to the passage of a particularly long freight train. I know that happens in this part of the country.
I recall going through the city of Brock-ville not long ago, and the traffic was held up in that place for some considerable time. So we are faced here with a grave problem. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the amount of money provided for this bill is totally inadequate even to come close to dealing with the problem. After all, this legislation must be judged in the light of its effectiveness in doing a job. When we realize the immensity of the job to be done, and when we look at the figure of $5 million, we appreciate how ineffective the legislation is going to be.
I suggest it is going to be ineffective, not only because of the paucity of the amount of money in the fund, but also because the municipalities are still to be called upon to bear a share, which not many of them are able to bear. I suggest that, in spite of the fact that these funds will now provide for a maximum of 60 per cent and that some arrangement may be reached with regard to the railroad's share, it is quite evident that a tremendous financial burden is going to be placed on the municipalities in this country. It does not matter what part of the country we consider, municipal councils and city councils have the same story to tell. The mill rate is now at an extremely high level and the municipal taxing authorities have gone as far as they can go. They are not able to undertake any appreciable expenditures of this kind.
Therefore, if the government suggests that through this legislation they are going to make any real attack on this problem, I think they have to give further consideration to the legislation. I do not know of any municipalities that are now in a position to

go to the board and ask that a particular project be undertaken, particularly when the average project in a city may involve an expenditure of a million dollars or more. The $5 million figure, I suggest, is in keeping with the procedure under which the money is made available, that the onus is on the municipalities. Instead of the board giving leadership, going out into the various parts of the country where the problem is most acute, and showing initiative, the initiative is going to have to be left to the municipalities, and not many municipalities are in a position at the present time to embark on an expenditure of a few hundred thousand dollars on a rail crossing project.
It seems to me that, in view of the position of the municipalities, if the government is anxious to bring about some improvement in the rail crossing problem in this country, then the government through the board is going to have to offer the leadership and supply most of the money. If that is not done, then I suggest that not many projects will be undertaken in the country at the present time. I want to repeat that there are not many municipalities in this country that are in a position today to go before the board with a recommended project and to proceed in the construction of that project when it is invariably going to cost them a good part of a million dollars on an average. So if the government is really anxious to do something about this problem, I suggest that the sum of money in the fund is going to have to be greatly increased; and secondly the board is going to have to be given wider latitude. It is going to have to be empowered to go out and seek to eradicate the problem where it is most serious and to take the initiative in proceeding with these projects. When I say "take the initiative", I suggest that it will of necessity involve offering to pay a larger share of the total cost than is provided for in the legislation.
There is one other matter which I wish to deal with. I touched on it on a previous occasion. I feel that, in view of the seriousness of the unemployment problem in Canada at the present time, the government should be casting about and seeking ways and means of providing employment and in so doing performing useful works throughout this country.
The hon. member for Danforth mentioned a moment ago the shelf of public works. We are familiar with the promises made by the government immediately after world war II, that, in the event that unemployment did come, the government would be prepared to provide employment through a shelf of public works. Since those public works have not
Railway Act
materialized, I feel that here, in at least a small sphere, the government could do something to provide immediate employment.
I realize that with modern methods of construction not too many actual labourers are going to be employed on these projects, but I suggest that where projects of this type are undertaken it is going to be a shot in the arm to business in localities where projects are being undertaken, and that it is going to assist in the economic welfare of the community. There are communities in every part of Canada that have problems of this kind, and the government could be using legislation to provide necessary jobs in those localities.
I was quite surprised a few weeks ago when the minister was commenting on the precedent set in the 1930's, when sums of money were made available in some cases from the unemployment relief fund to the rail crossing fund, and the minister at that time suggested that the time was not ripe. I asked him on that occasion whether he did not feel that now is the proper time to put sufficient money into the fund to provide some jobs. I must say that I was quite amazed by the answer given by the minister when he told the house that the government did not consider that now was the appropriate time to do anything in this regard. Now, I am just wondering how serious the situation is going to have to get in this country before the government is prepared to undertake even a small measure of this kind.
After all, we can talk about unemployment, we can talk about the necessity of providing jobs, but here is one specific example of where the government could be doing some little thing at least towards providing employment; and yet they feel that now is not the appropriate time. They are prepared to wait until the unemployment situation, I presume, gets worse. So I want to urge the minister at this stage to give serious consideration to the suggestions which have been made and to reconsider his earlier answer that the time has not yet arrived when it might be deemed necessary or advisable to place in this fund additional sums of money with the specific purpose of making an attack on the unemployment problem to at least a small extent in some parts of the country. I want to urge the minister to consider very seriously just how effective this legislation is going to be. We all welcome the addition of $5 million, but at the same time we have to ask ourselves this question. As a result of this legislation, will grade separation projects be undertaken in this country? That is the acid test of the legislation. I suggest that under the present arrangement, where the municipalities are called

Railway Act
upon to pay an extremely heavy burden as part of the costs, not many subways are going to be built; and after all that is the real test of the legislation.
It is my considered opinion that if the government is willing to grant the board greater latitude and to permit it to enter into negotiations with the municipalities with a view to undertaking projects where perhaps the board would pay 100 per cent of the cost and relieve the municipalities in needy cases of any expense whatsoever, then we are going to do something about eliminating grade crossings in this country. But if we are simply going to pass the buck to the municipalities and limit the funds to $5 million and expect the municipality to come along with a few hundred thousand dollars to undertake the project, then this money is going to stay in the fund for some time. I can understand why the government decided that the money was not to be allowed to accumulate beyond $7 million. So I urge the government at this time to give some serious reconsideration to the bill in its present form and to bring forward the changes which, in my opinion, will make it more effective.

subtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this subject was quite broadly discussed during the resolution stage and I do not pretend that at this point one can add new considerations, but in connection with the problem there are several factors on which I should like to lay stress briefly this afternoon.
We have three principal aspects of the bill. First, there is the increase in the annual parliamentary contribution to the railway grade crossing fund from $1 million to $5 million. Second, there is the increase from 40 to 60 per cent which may be ordered by the board of transport commissioners to be paid out of that fund, toward the cost of construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public. Then, third, there is the increase from $150,000 to $300,000 in the ceiling on the contribution which may be paid out of the grade crossing fund to the cost of construction of any such project.
The measure has been welcomed in all parts of the house; indeed, Mr. Speaker, it has received warm approval as far as it goes. The discussion has been concerned largely with pointing out what may be inadequacies in it and with urging upon the government an increase in the provisions thus made.
The two features which have attracted attention in the discussion have been safety of the public and some assistance in the attack on the unemployment problem. Both of these are serious matters deserving of the highest degree of attention on the part of

parliament. As to safety, one need not dwell at length on the huge economic cost of injuries and fatalities in crossing accidents. It is easy enough for us to think of investments on the part of the public and those others who are called upon to contribute substantial amounts to the cost of grade crossing projects. Against that consideration, however, must be placed, in redress of the ledger balance, the huge annual economic cost of fatalities and injuries inflicted year by year in crossing accidents which might otherwise be avoided; and that is quite apart from the anguish that is caused by reason of those fatalities and injuries.
In the excellent and comprehensive report which the board of transport commissioners submitted to the minister on this subject, they brought most of their figures down to the end of the year 1953. I have obtained some of the figures for the year 1954 with a view to bringing the information up to date. Out of the large numbers of injuries and fatalities in the course of railway accidents, these figures have been isolated as applicable to accidents arising at public highway crossings, regardless of the form of protection or whether protection there exists. In 1954 at public highway crossings on railways there were 454 accidents involving injuries to persons, and in those accidents 179 people were killed and 596 were injured. That is a formidable total indeed. How does it compare with the record in recent years? I have here the figures on the number of accidents at the same types of crossings in the five-year period commencing with 1950. In 1950 there were 457 accidents at these public highway crossings; in 1951, there were 490; in 1952, there were 463; in 1953, there were 487 and in 1954 there were 454.
What has been the contribution to the solution of this problem by various types of crossing protection? A further glance at these figures indicates that over three-quarters of these accidents which have occurred at public highway crossings on railways have occurred at unprotected crossings. In 1950, out of the 457 accidents, 356 occurred at unprotected crossings; in 1951, out of the 490 accidents, 393 occurred at unprotected crossings; in 1952, out of 463 accidents, 364 occurred at unprotected crossings; in 1953, out of the 487 accidents, 392 occurred at unprotected crossings; and in 1954, out of the 454 accidents, 353 occurred at unprotected crossings.
Density of population and also density of motor car traffic enter into the picture substantially, as one can see by looking at the breakdown of the numbers of accidents at such crossings by provinces. These figures indicate that well over 40 per cent of accidents

at grade crossings have occurred in the province of Ontario where population is more dense and the numbers of motor cars are so much larger.
On the part of some, Mr. Speaker, there is an impression that, after all, most of these accidents occur at night and that people keep their eyes open in the daytime. The figures do not bear out any such impression. Taking the figures for 1954, one finds that, out of the 454 accidents to which I referred, 235 of them occurred during daylight hours and only 219 during the night hours. In the case of accidents that occurred where motor vehicles were struck by a train-and of these there were 264-150 of them occurred during daylight hours and 114 during night hours. Those are cases where the collisions took the form of the train striking the motor vehicle. The majority of them occurred in daylight. No doubt many of them were cases where people had tried to beat the train across the crossing and others where they failed to observe the approach of the train. Then in the case of accidents that took the form of motor vehicles running into the side of trains-and there are many of these accidents-last year there were 140 of them, of which 46 occurred in daylight hours and 94 during the night hours.
It seems to me that these are important statistics, Mr. Speaker. The cost of grade separation work-indeed the cost of "construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public", to follow the words of the statute-is unquestionably high. Whether these works take the form of complete grade separation or of other crossing protection, the construction of these works is becoming increasingly costly year by year. The cost of constructing those projects-some of them major projects-has particularly increased by leaps and bounds with the soaring cost of construction in recent years. Consequently, with the increase in cost there has been a natural resistance, on the part of municipalities and oftentimes on the part of railways, to projects of this kind. Therefore, the importance of the increase in the permissible contribution from the grade crossing fund, from 40 per cent to 60 per cent in these cases, is, in my humble opinion, fully as important as is the increase in the annual contribution from $1 million to $5 million.
It would really be of much less effect than I think many hon. members of the house assume if the annual contribution were multiplied fivefold in this way and if there were not at the same time a corresponding increase in the maximum percentage which the board of transport commissioners may order to be paid out of the crossing fund to the cost 50433-184
Railway Act
of construction of any of these projects. Let us remember, sir, that the number of those among whom the cost of the work may be assessed is not large. In the case of provincial highways you have the provinces. In the case of other highways, and sometimes also in the case of provincial highways, you have the municipalities. Then you have the railways and you sometimes have public utilities. You sometimes have electric or street railways.
Let us bear in mind that no portion of the cost of maintenance of these crossings is paid out of the railway grade crossing fund and that when any of these projects is ordered to be constructed those upon whom a portion of the cost is assessed must face the fact that along with that allocation goes an allocation of the cost of future maintenance, and in many cases that may be a sizeable sum.
But let us look at this matter of the maximum contribution to the cost of construction as distinguished from the cost of maintenance. It is a heavy burden indeed that can be created for municipalities and for railways under these orders. So far as I am aware we have not, in any of the tables in the report of the board of transport commissioners, the total amount which has thus far been levied against any of the individual railways operating in Canada. We may see in the report at page 27, for instance, that the total expenditure for protection at highway crossings from 1909, the date of the inception of the railway grade crossing fund, down to the end of 1953 was approximately $52 million, and it appears that something over $18 million was assessed against the railways as their portion of the total. I think if further inquiry were made into the figures, including the cost of maintenance, we would have a much clearer picture than is yet available of the very formidable cost laid upon the railways in relation to the construction and maintenance of such projects.
As to the municipalities, the table on page 27 to which I have referred does not distinguish between provinces and municipalities, but out of the $52 million aggregate the total of contributions levied against the provinces and municipalities from 1909 to 1953 exceeds $19 million. Sir, this amount is bound to rise as the total increases if there is not some change made now along the lines proposed by which the proportion of the cost that may be paid out of the railway grade crossing fund may be increased.
One does not say that the experience of Canadian railways is precisely parallel to that of the United States railways operating in densely built up areas, but I mention the

Railway Act
experience of one railway in the United States. It is not completely transcontinental, but one important railway in the United States having an annual business approximating that of Canadian National Railways or Canadian Pacific Railway has had levies upon it so far for grade separation and railway grade crossing works exceeding $160 million. It is time that we stopped and observed the warning in relation to this cost.
As long as municipalities are to be called upon to bear a substantial percentage of the cost of construction, they, in their depressed condition, are bound to offer resistance in many cases. It does not matter that in so many of these cases the need of the grade separation or of some change in the form of crossing protection is acknowledged. Accidents may have resulted at a crossing by reason of the absence of some better form of protection but in case after case-and I speak out of not a little experience in relation to cases of this kind-one finds objections taken by the municipalities simply because they feel they cannot meet the percentage of cost that is proposed to be levied upon them.
A similar situation exists in the case of the railways, which are a depressed industry in Canada today. We are reminded of that in the recent report of the royal commission on agreed charges by the former Mr. Justice Turgeon. He points to the fact that the railways of Canada today are a depressed industry. When the railways are called upon to pay substantial percentages towards the cost of construction of these works, is it any wonder, when these costs far exceed any benefit that the railway may expect to derive from the crossing protection or grade separation, that the railways in many cases are obliged to resist? That leads me to say this. We hear discussion in the chamber about the great potential value of a general program of crossing protection and grade separation in Canada as an aid to relieve unemployment, but it is of little value to propose that great national schemes of this kind should be undertaken if we are going to be faced with the same type of allocation of costs as we have been facing hitherto. It only means that the more of these projects that are mooted the stronger must be the objections taken by the municipalities affected and the stronger the objections that must be taken by the railways that are affected so long as the amount that they are called upon to contribute exceeds the benefit that they receive from the contemplated construction.
The increase from 40 per cent to 60 per cent in the proportion that may be paid out

of the railway grade crossing fund is, in my estimation, as important as any other feature contained in this measure. I point out to the house that the 60 per cent we are now about to legislate is a maximum, just as the 40 per cent was that has existed in recent years. There is no guarantee that the board of transport commissioners will award that sum to be paid out of the grade crossing fund in every case that comes before it. It simply means that parliament is giving power to the board to order up to 60 per cent of the cost of construction to be paid in any case where it meets with the board's approval to do so.
If there is going to be an attempt made in the interests of public safety or public convenience to expand the program of grade separation works in Canada, then I think we must be prepared to be more generous in order to lighten the burden on the municipalities in those cases and, so far as the railways are concerned, it seems to me we must be prepared to draw more guidance from the policy being followed in the United States. It is federal policy in the United States to limit the contribution that the railways are called upon to make to grade separation in two ways: first of all, to limit the contribution to the benefit to be received by the railway from the contemplated construction and, second, even to limit that to an aggregate of 10 per cent of the total cost.
The federal policy in the United States thus provides for railways to participate in the cost of projects according to the benefits they receive and subject to this maximum of 10 per cent of the total cost. If there are no benefits available to the railways as a result of the projected grade separation, the railways are not called upon to contribute anything to the cost of grade separation in the United States. That is the federal policy there.
Now, the policy of the states is not uniform in this matter. There is quite a wide variation in the legislative policy of the various state legislatures in those cases where the grade separation falls within state, rather than federal, jurisdiction. There are some states which have laws providing for an allocation of cost according to the benefits received, which is like the federal policy in that country. Some states have placed a maximum of 15 per cent on the total contribution that may be levied upon the railways. Other states provide that the railways may be called upon to contribute a fixed percentage ranging from 10 per cent to 20 per cent. In other states, the state commission has the power to fix the railway contributions

in a manner somewhat similar to the provision made in our own Railway Act, within certain limits.
It is well for us to bear in mind, sir, the increasing extent to which benefit has been made the yardstick of the contribution that the railways in the United States have been called upon to make towards the cost of grade separation- work. In Canada there has been a steady and beneficial trend over the long period since 1909. Canada began in 1909 with a maximum contribution from the railway grade crossing fund of 20 per cent. In 1919 this contribution was increased to 25 per cent, and in 1926 to 40 per cent. It has remained at 40 per cent for 19 long years. The measure that is before us now has indeed been delayed too long.
Accompanying these percentage maxima there have been as well absolute maxima imposed in connection with the cost of any project, beginning in 1909 with $5,000. This was increased, the last time in 1950, to $150,000 per project which was far too low because the construction costs of these projects, oftentimes in areas where they are most needed, have run to such high figures that the maximum contribution of $150,000 out of the fund has been quite inadequate. I have misgivings also, Mr. Speaker, as to the adequacy of the proposed maximum of $300,000 per project.
When I raised this point in the debate in 1950, pointing out that the maximum contribution of $150,000 from the railway grade crossing fund was going to have the effect of preventing the elimination of grade crossings in some important situations, I was told that the great danger was that if we did not impose such a maximum the result could be that a few costly projects could absorb the entire amount available in the railway grade crossing fund. Now we are having a fivefold increase in the annual contribution, we are having an increase from 40 per cent to 60 per cent in the percentage contributions of the fund. I question whether the proposed new maximum of $300,000 for any one project is justified.
Looking back over the years, it is well that we bear in mind that on more than one occasion the railway grade crossing fund has been exhausted. It is well that we should bear in mind also that its purpose is more than safety. The terms of the statute contemplate the use of the fund for construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public. Undoubtedly, to an increasing extent, grade eliminations are being sought not merely in the interests of public safety, but in the interests of speed and public convenience. The great increase 50433-184$
Railway Act
in the volume of motor traffic on our highways has resulted in many cases in a stimulated demand for the elimination of grade crossings. That is a factor that must be recognized, and it is another reason why an increasing percentage of the cost of crossing eliminations should be borne at public expense rather than at the expense of these municipalities, railways, public utilities or others who are, in the language of the statute, interested or affected by the proposed crossing works.
Sir, the problem is great. It is a problem that is bound to increase in proportion with the increase in highway traffic in Canada. I hope that no one will pretend that the increases that are being made in the bill are adequate to meet the problem. They are an important and valuable step forward. One would commend the report of the board of transport commissioners, and the recommendations which they have put before the government and to which, with one exception, effect is being given by this legislation. I am bold enough to predict, sir, that further legislative changes lie before us as we realize the extent to which this is a public problem and not simply the problem of the municipalities or the railways or the public utilities immediately affected in the case of any project. We would do well, it seems to me, to draw benefit and guidance from the example of the United States in this regard.

I do not wish to take up the time of the house, Mr. Speaker, by reciting what has already been so adequately dealt with by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and others who have criticized the suggested legislation. It is sufficient to say that we are all, of course, glad to see that the government has taken steps to increase the amount of this fund and increase the proportion of the contribution. We all realize this is necessary because of the increase in highway traffic in Canada and the speeding up of that traffic. In addition there seems little doubt that the already overtaxed municipalities are going to have to pay a still larger proportion of the cost of these enterprises.
There is only one thing in this bill with which I should like to deal, and that is the method of initiating proceedings. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) made the following statement as recorded on page 2134 of Hansard for March 17, 1955:
The board of transport commissioners, which administers the fund, does not itself initiate the execution of these projects, but acts upon the petition of a railway company, a municipality, a province or some other interest that desires to have the project carried out.

Railway Act
Now, having a very dangerous crossing in my own constituency, which I have mentioned many times in this house, I have had conversations with members of the board of transport commissioners or rather officers of that board. It is my understanding that often proceedings of this sort are initiated by the board itself, either as the result of reports of traffic accidents or as a result of reports by the board's inspectors. Possibly when the minister replies he will make a further statement in the matter. This whole discussion came up, may 1 say, as a result of certain inquiries I have had occasion to make.
Since the sum the board has at its disposal for the construction of grade crossings is to be greatly increased, I trust the records kept by the board will be improved. I mention this because only recently I placed a question on the order paper, which was set out in Votes and Proceedings No. 52 at page "i", the issue of March 21, 1955. The subject was that of the Canadian National Railways crossing near Woodstock, Ontario.
The question was set out as follows:'
1.	Have any accidents occurred, since September 26, 1947, at the crossing where the main line of the Canadian National Railways from Montreal to Chicago crossed the Ontario provincial highway No. 2, approximately seven miles east of Woodstock? If so, how many?
2.	Has the board of transport commissioners considered giving assistance from the railway crossing fund towards the construction of an underpass at this point?
3.	If so, has the board yet reached a decision, and in what respect?
The answer given to me is as follows:
The board has no record of any accidents at this crossing since September 26,	1947. This
crossing is automatically protected with a wigwag and bells and to date no application has been received by the board for construction of a grade separation at this crossing.
The latter part of the answer is quite correct when it states that the crossing is protected by a wigwag and bells, and that no application has been made. However, it is my understanding, from information I have received from officials of the board, that, since this is a provincial highway, application would more properly be made to the province. This has not been done as yet.
I cannot understand however the first part of the answer, where it says-
The board has no record of any accidents at this crossing since September 26, 1947.
After receiving the answer I took the trouble to get in touch with the board by telephone, stating that I was somewhat surprised by the answer given, and suggesting that they make a further check and make another reply. The answer I received orally was much the same as the one I had received to the question I had placed on the order paper.

I have discussed this matter before, and the board must have some record of it. At the first session of this twenty-second parliament I raised the matter in the house on three different occasions, as indicated at pages 5167, 5615 and 6080 of Hansard for that session. Dear Mr. Chevrier:
For your interest and information I am enclosing clipping from the Daily Sentinel Review, Woodstock, for Tuesday, June 22nd, with respect to my favorite railway crossing at Creditville near Woodstock.
The reply received from the then minister on June 28 is as follows:

I trust that you will refer this matter for consideration to Mr. Donald Gordon.
The minister's reply under date of June 14, 1954, is in these words:
Dear Mr. Nesbitt:
I have your letter of June 10th with which you enclose a clipping from the London Free Press dealing with an accident at the underpass of the Canadian National main line seven miles east of Woodstock.
Then, under date of June 17, 1954, I have this notice from the board of transport commissioners:

In view of what I have just read, and the statements I have made, I find it difficult to understand how such an answer could have been given to the question I placed on the order paper. May I say that I have since been able to make inquiries from the Ontario provincial police which indicate that between Friday, September 26, 1947, and Saturday, February 5, 1955, there have been 77 accidents at this railway crossing in which 28 persons have been injured and one killed.
I do not wish to take further time of the house, but it must be obvious to everyone that this crossing is exceedingly dangerous; and I would hope that in the near future it would be dealt with by the board of transport commissioners, if it is within their power to do so. Mr. Daniel Mclvor <Fori William): Mr. Speaker, I have much pleasure in commending the board of transport commissioners for pushing this increase, and the minister for co-operating with the board.
In the last 20 years I have had many dealings with the board and I must say that never once have I been disappointed with what they have done. Sometimes I did not get what I asked for, but at times I have found that the action taken by the board was better than that I had recommended.
In ward 1 of Fort William we had a very dangerous crossing, and for years there had been agitation to have a subway built. There were many tracks children had to cross when going to and from school. Ambulances and doctors were in no better position; they too had to wait.
When the position was placed clearly and forcefully before the board of transport commissioners no difficulty was encountered at all. This was done at a cost of $100,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway, a similar amount to the city of Fort William, and $100,000 to the dominion government. I realize of course that other cities are not as fortunate in their city council as is the city of Fort William, where finances are handled in splendid fashion. The city paid $100,000 and the government paid $100,000 and now we are well protected. The
Railway Act
citizens of ward 1 are grateful to the members of the transport board, to the Canadian Pacific Railway and to the government.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few brief observations on this bill and to express my support of this legislation. The addition of the $5 million to the fund is to be welcomed and also the increase of the percentage to 60 per cent to be paid by the board and raising the maximum contribution to $300,000. That is all to the good.
Like some of the previous speakers, I wish the government had seen fit to increase the annual contribution to the fund; but, Mr. Speaker, I cannot resist the opportunity at this moment to point out to the house that the hon. gentlemen to my right, the members of the Progressive Conservative party, are some of the most illogical people I have ever listened to. On nearly every measure that comes before this house, they ask the government to increase its contribution to the legislation concerned, and when the budget comes down they howl at the government to reduce taxation. You cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. We of this group realize the necessity for taxation. All we ask is a fairer redistribution of the sums collected in taxation. The hon. gentlemen to my right are somewhat inconsistent in their approach.
However, I do wish to bring to the minister's attention the fact that in my constituency there are quite dangerous railroad crossings that go through quite small village municipalities, municipalities so small that it would be completely beyond their capacity to enter into any arrangements for the building of an underpass, an overpass or anything of that sort. Because the problem is so general in Canada, I realize it is not possible to think of anything being done for some years to come. But I do want to suggest to

Railway Act
the minister that a relatively small expenditure on more vivid marking of crossings or the lighting of crossings at night, an expenditure that would be small compared with the expenditure required to build an overpass or an underpass, would be of great help. On many crossings there is simply a railroad crossing sign and nothing else. I suggest that in places where it is not possible at the present time to undertake those larger works, much more could be done with small expenditures to bring to the public's attention the fact that they are approaching a railroad crossing. The signs could be more dramatic in the daytime and they could be lit up at night. More could be done in that respect.
I have travelled over a number of crossings from time to time and I have realized how meagre the warning was that one was approaching a crossing where one might meet a freight train, particularly a freight train in my case, at any hour of the day or night. Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much my ability to answer the hon. member for Kootenay West in connection with the blanket criticism of the Conservative party. However, I might mention that it is possible to recommend additional expenditures of money on a fairer basis than is provided by the present tax structure that we have and still criticize the budget which has been brought down. I might say to the hon. member that he neglected to add the additional fact that this party believes many millions of dollars are available if the proper economical type of government is provided for this country. However, I want to deal with one or two questions only. I am sure the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) will be very happy because he expressed himself in that way when I rose the last time.
We should remember that the figures we are dealing with are very misleading. If we check the history of this legislation we find that the initial contribution of the federal government was $5,000 for each project. That has been raised to $15,000 and $25,000. In 1928 it was raised to $100,000 and in 1950, to $150,000. I am wondering whether when we talk about $300,000-and my friends to my left continue to refer to this item-we take into account the serious inflation we have had in this country during those years. If we went back to the early years of this century and talked about $5,000, I am wondering whether it did not provide as much as the
[Mr. Herridge.3
$300,000 will provide that we are talking about today. That restriction is a very serious one in connection with the complicated type of grade separation we have in the larger metropolitan areas. Of course, the same criticism in connection with the increase from $1 million to $5 million in the total allocation to the fund would be a reasonable one. To a great extent the government is simply keeping up with the increased cost of this type of construction, and is not taking into account the thousands and thousands of additional motor vehicles that use the highways every year.
At the resolution stage I pointed out that this government collected approximately $250 million in various types of taxes from the motor-driving public. I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has reduced certain of the taxes on vehicles and has removed the tax on automobile tires and items of that kind, but this government still extracts from the motorists at least $200 million each year. As far as I can determine, it spends only $15 million a year on them. It is about time that some consideration was given to the motorist. He is paying the taxes; he should be provided with safety facilities to the extent that he provides the government treasury with dollars. Even with the tax reductions, the Minister of Finance is counting on an increased sale of motor vehicles to provide him with the same net amount of taxes that he was able to get last year. It would seem logical to me that the amount of money to be applied by the federal government to this fund should be tied in some way to the taxes that are collected from the motor-driving public. If a percentage formula were arrived at, at an adequate amount, it would provide for the additional vehicles which will undoubtedly be on the highways of this country in the future. There is no end to them. Over the week end I noticed in the press it is expected that in the next four or five years about half the families in the United States will have two automobiles. If that is the case there, I am quite satisfied that the same trend will take place here. Surely, I might say to the Minister of National Revenue, it is just as logical to have a fund of this kind tied to the sales tax collected on automobiles, because of the increased sale of automobiles, as it is to provide for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to receive the sales tax collected on television receivers. As a matter of fact it is probably much more logical when we look at the balance sheet of that corporation and find that it can pass over $6 or $7 million of taxes collected to be used in some future year at the whim and fancy of the corporation.

The second point with which I wish to deal has been referred to on numerous occasions by other speakers. The hon. member for Kootenay West again referred to the fact that what we are asking for here is a redistribution of the taxation base, and undoubtedly it is the municipalities who are having the difficulty in providing safety facilities of this type for the public. Until such time as a reassessment of taxing powers can be reached by agreement among all three levels of government, the municipalities are going to find themselves in a very difficult position. I have said this before, and I say it again. Their tax base is so close to them that they find it impossible to take advantage quickly of the various new people coming to the country who are paying sales tax on the items they buy and who are paying income tax by deductions from their pay immediately they begin to work. The municipalities have no such opportunity, and they are being placed in an increasingly difficult financial situation, which is pressing them to the utmost.
I have one further point. When the federal-provincial conference which has been called for the next week or so is brought together here in Ottawa, the federal authorities would be very well advised to suggest as part of the agenda increasing the contribution to be made to the grade separation fund by a reallocation of taxing powers for that purpose. This would also help meet some of the other pressing problems.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to try to deal very briefly with some of the arguments which have been advanced during the course of the debate.
The first refers to the question of the increase from $1 million to $5 million in the annual appropriation to the grade crossing fund. On the part of a number of speakers the opinion has been expressed that this increase from $1 million to $5 million is inadequate and that it will not be possible with that amount to solve the problem arising from the existence of the many unprotected grade crossings which we have in Canada. As I think I said the other day in discussing the resolution, I do not believe
Railway Act
anybody would seriously consider that it would be possible, by merely appropriating an amount of $5 million a year, to solve the whole problem of grade crossings. The number which exists and the cost of even the simplest form of protection, I think, show how foolish it would be for anyone to believe that the mere provision of an increase from $1 million to $5 million annually would mean the end of the problem.
I would like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that the amount of $5 million was suggested in the report of the board of transport commissioners. I think the reasons which they have given are very eloquent and explain fully why the amount has not been made larger. I think it will be seen from reading the report that this might be regarded as an experimental figure. I wonder if I might read two extracts from the report, Mr. Speaker. The first of these appears on page 90 of the typewritten report, and is as follows:
In attempting to determine what might be the annual federal contribution to the fund, we recognize that while it cannot be determined with mathematical precision, it must reasonably reflect the practical aspects of the matter. Any amount which may be arrived at we think should also be sufficiently flexible in character to admit of modification in the light of actual experience. It would be difficult to justify a federal contribution which was not in reasonable accordance with the availability of highway authority funds. Certainly it would be uneconomic to cause a diversion of highway funds to grade crossing improvements in an amount which was not commensurate with the magnitude of the crossing problem. At the same time an increase in the contribution of the federal government, when related to the percentage distribution of costs as hereinbefore recommended would necessarily result in increasing the total potential costs to other parties-and regard must be had to the increased costs which the other parties may be economically justified in assuming. Furthermore, while we are aware that some provinces have sufficient funds to enable them to undertake a sizeable crossing improvement program, we cannot use their preferred position as a criterion of what other provinces may be able to undertake.
If I may summarize, Mr. Speaker, it was after long experience in administering the grade crossing fund that the board came forward with the recommendation that the annual amount be increased from $1 million to $5 million.
The report of the board continues to deal with the aspect to which some hon. members have referred, namely the fact that if in any year there is an uncommitted balance of $2 million or more, the appropriation for that year is to be reduced; that is obviously intended not to cut down on the expenditures but to avoid putting in the fund moneys not actually required for the purposes of the fund itself. The suggestion is that of the board, and I think it was quite obviously made in

Railway Act
order to avoid placing in the fund moneys for which they see no immediate use.
I would like to conclude my reading of some extracts from the report with these two phrases, which I think are rather significant. They say, speaking of course of the amount of $5 million:
The sum which we now propose cannot be regarded otherwise than an estimate of probable demands on the fund under the new conditions. It may well be two or three years before the most effective amount of the annual appropriation can be more definitely fixed.
That is the reason, Mr. Speaker, I said I thought that the amount of $5 million might be looked upon as being experimental.
The hon. member for Eglinton mentioned two other important features of this legislation, though I was not quite sure that the full significance of these changes had been fully grasped by him. The first was his reference to the increase in the percentage of the contribution of the railway grade crossing fund. He spoke of it, I think quite properly, as an improvement and said it is quite obvious that the increase of the contribution from 40 to 60 per cent will provide corresponding relief to the others who must also make contributions toward a project. But I think it must also be taken into account in connection with the other increase to which he also referred. That was the increase of, let us say, the maximum base for any project from $150,000 to $300,000.
I think we must not forget that these two changes are being made at the same time, so there is really a much more substantial increase in the contribution from the fund than would appear at first sight. For example, under the law as it stands at the present time, if a project costs $500,000 the maximum base is $150,000 and the contribution of the board would represent 40 per cent of that amount or $60,000. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RADIO ANTENNAE AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 260, to amend the Radio Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RADIO ANTENNAE AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES
speechtext:
Yes. Mr. Speaker, as I explained to the house in introducing the resolution which preceded this legislation it is proposed to make three amendments to the Radio Act. The first of these amendments would empower the Minister of Transport to make regulations regarding antennae for radio stations and private receiving stations. As it is somewhat complex I shall give a full explanation of the purposes we have in mind in proposing it.
Hon. members will agree, I am sure, that with the advent of television and the development of the elaborate outdoor aerials now commonly used, it would be desirable to take measures to control their mechanical features for safety purposes from the point of view of air navigation and protection of life and property. Because of its responsibilities for civil aviation and radio my department naturally is anxious to see that in the installation, erection, construction and repair of antennae, proper standards are maintained; but several municipalities and one of the provinces have also evinced interest in the matter by inquiries as to the making of bylaws governing television antennae.
It seems quite clear that the regulation of antennae is a part of the general field of radio regulation and, therefore, within the legislative competence of parliament. If confirmation of this assertion were necessary it would be found in the fact that in a number of localities in Canada television sets cannot operate without external antennae. Legislative authority in the matter being vested in parliament, we believe that the requisite legislation should be adopted to enable the Minister of Transport to establish the necessary regulations. The authority to make regulations would extend both to radio stations and to private receiving stations as defined in the Radio Act.
We have a measure of control at the present time over antennae for radio stations in that in administering the licensing provisions of the Radio Act we may control the nature and type of the antennae to be used, but we believe that it would be desirable to have general regulations respecting antennae that would be applicable to the various classes of radio stations. Though formerly the department had, through licensing, some control over private receiving stations, now that licensing of these stations has been abolished we no longer have any control over the antennae used by them.
In this connection I should like to tell hon. members that we propose to use as a basis for our regulations respecting the mechanical features of antennae for private receiving stations a set of standards for receiving 50433-185
Radio Act
antennae already prepared by the Canadian standards association which, as many hon. members know, is an industrial group which enjoys an excellent reputation because of the numerous standards it has laid down for the electrical and other fields.
I think I should make it quite clear that it is not our present intention to make these regulations concerning the mechanical features applicable generally, but only in those municipalities where the municipal authorities desire that they be made applicable and wish to undertake the responsibility of administration and enforcement. In these cases we contemplate appointing as inspectors under the act the municipal officials who carry out building inspection in the municipalities. We believe that arrangements along these lines would satisfy the municipalities which wish to see some control exercised over the elaborate antennae now being used.
Hon. members, therefore, will appreciate that in the circumstances we are not contemplating adding large numbers to the staff of the telecommunications division of my department for the administration of the proposed regulations. In fact at the present time I do not expect that any increase in staff will be necessary for this particular purpose.
The second of the amendments to be made by the present bill would empower the minister to adopt regulations exempting from licensing requirements numerous low-powered radio devices which technically constitute radio stations within the meaning of the Radio Act. Many hon. members are familiar with mechanical equipment such as doors in railway stations, garage doors, etc., which are actuated by an electric eye, and with interoffice communication systems which are not dependent upon the use of wires. I am sure hon. members will agree that it would be desirable to exempt the owners or operators of such devices from the necessity of obtaining a licence for them.
If this amendment is accepted it is intended to adopt specifications determining the maximum signal strength of the device that will be exempt. In this way we will avoid exempting devices that would interfere with radio reception and manufacturers will know that devices meeting these specifications will be exempt from licensing.
The purpose of the third amendment is to implement the obligations assumed by Canada under the international telecommunication convention with respect to the preservation of the secrecy of radio communications. By this convention Canada is obligated to impose secrecy restrictions on all radio communications not intended for the general use of the public.

Radio Act
At the present time the Radio Act provides that operators of coast or land stations or of mobile stations must subscribe to a declaration of secrecy, and the act prescribes penalties against such operators for the unauthorized use of information obtained by interception of any radio communication. The act also empowers the minister to make regulations to provide against any person divulging information received by means of a private receiving station. There is, however, a loophole which it seems desirable to close. Any individual can buy equipment that will permit him to receive practically any radio signal regardless of its frequency or wave length, and so to intercept private communications outside the ordinary or normal broadcast band. A receiver embodying this equipment does not fall clearly within the definition of a coast or land station or mobile station or a private receiving station, and consequently the operator is not subject either to the necessity of subscribing to a declaration of secrecy or to the regulations against divulging information applicable to operators of private receiving stations.
We do not propose by the amendment to prevent the ordinary private citizen from operating shortwave or other receiving sets; all we say is that, having become acquainted with any radio communication not intended for public use or information, a person may not make use of it or divulge it to any person.
In recommending this amendment we wish, of course, to implement and fulfil Canada's obligations under the convention to which I referred a moment ago, but we also wish to satisfy the complaints we have received in my department against the misuse of private communications.
In conclusion may I point out that questions concerning interference in the radio field, control of manufacturers and community television receiving systems are not within the scope of the present legislation. If hon. members wish to deal with these particular subjects I suggest that they might do so when the estimates of my department are under consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING TRACKS IN TORONTO HARBOUR AREA
speechtext:
There is not much I can add at this time to the statement I made at the resolution stage of this measure. As hon. members will no doubt recall, this simple bill seeks the ratification and confirmation by parliament of an agreement entered into last fall between the Toronto harbour commissioners, the Toronto Terminals Railway Company, Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Rilway Company. This agreement has to do with the rehabilitation and maintenance of railway tracks built by the Toronto harbour commissioners for the purpose of serving industries located in the harbour area. Since the commission did not have sufficient funds to maintain and rehabilitate these tracks, they approached the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways with the object of having them take over the rehabilitation and maintenance thereof.
An agreement was therefore entered into to that effect on October 5, 1954. Since the Toronto Terminals Railway Company is not

empowered under its act of incorporation, chapter 170 of the statutes of 1906, to enter into such agreements, the present bill seeks to amend the act accordingly.
I wish to add at this time that it is proposed to move that the measure be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, after it has received second reading.

subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING TRACKS IN TORONTO HARBOUR AREA
