Mr. Speaker, we are pleased that we will have an opportunity in the standing committee to give closer scrutiny to this legislation. The parliamentary assistant has given the assurance that schedule A, indicating the additional lands involved in connection with the trackages, will be made available to us at that time.
Any member from the greater Toronto district is definitely interested in anything affecting the harbour area of that city. I know we will receive a full explanation of the clauses of the bill. I do feel some concern, however, about the fact that the commission may lose some of its power to do what it may wish in connection with some phases of development in that harbour area. I refer to those powers to which reference is made in the agreement between the terminals railway company and the commission.
The agreement involved in the legislation simply makes provision for funds which formerly were not available to the commission for the rehabilitation of trackage, and makes a further provision for the extension of such trackage. Under the terms of the agreement such trackage extension will be paid for by the commission, and one would assume therefore that they are sufficiently in funds to take care of that aspect of the situation confronting them.
I am not sure this could not have been done by a simple amendment permitting the making of a loan to the harbour commission during the strenuous period through which they are passing. Undoubtedly there will be tremendous expansion in the Toronto harbour area, and it seems to me that some type of loan could have been made. After all, this money has been put up by the Toronto Terminals Railway Company only on a temporary basis. It is to be collected back over a period of ten years through the imposition of fees on carloadings charged to the two major railway companies.
I believe these same features could have been handled by the commission, and it could have retained strict control of the development if a loan of the kind I have mentioned had been made to it. In this way they would not have lost any of the area in which they exercise discretionary powers.
Railways
I realize that the extensions are to be by agreement, and that decisions are to be made by arbitration if no other means is successful. However, there are sections in the bill I find difficult to understand. For instance, there is the provision for the disposal of used material. I assume this would be in the form of trackage taken up. It appears that this used material is to be left for disposal by the commission. It seems obvious that the terminals railway company and the two national railways would have much better facilities for disposing of this kind of equipment, and I find it difficult to understand why the commission should be handling it.
I also note that interest on this money is to be charged monthly, a provision which seems somewhat unusual. Under an act of the province of Ontario interest can be calculated only on a quarterly basis. I do not see much difference between this legislation and legislation of other kinds under which money would be obtained.
Perhaps because I, too, am a lessee of property under the control of the harbour commission I have some concern over the fact that in the legislation the terminals railway company and the two national railways involved in the agreement are exempted from the payment of municipal taxes. It is indicated that the commission will undertake this burden for the three railway companies. I am sure I would be very happy if they would extend this privilege, because it would certainly relieve the burden on many taxpayers in that area.
I do not see why the bill should contain a provision of that kind. It would seem that this is a straight business transaction under which the terminals railway company is to be placed in possession and is to have the full advantages of the use of the land in question for a period of ten years. It is to be permitted to collect tolls which, in turn, will pay for the rental of the trackage in the area. I suggest therefore that it might be worth while to take a second look at that provision.
I said earlier that we would have an opportunity of considering the bill clause by clause. Before taking my seat, however, I would like to add that a tremendous job has been done in Toronto by the commission in connection with the development of the waterfront area. However, a problem of great magnitude is now facing them. I am not suggesting that they have not faced great problems before; but we know that in view of the development of the St. Lawrence seaway the position held by the commission in Toronto becomes of vital importance to that city.	-

Railways
I am reluctant to see the removal of any authority or discretionary powers the commission may have in connection with the development of the area. Of course until we have schedule A before us we cannot know exactly what provisions are being made for the development to take place. The commission is already facing serious problems when it meets other authorities. The municipality of metropolitan Toronto has had super highways designed which will cross the area, and which I am sure the commission will not regard as helpful to the enhancement and proper development of the area. As a matter of fact, instead of taking away any discretionary power, probably they should be in a position even to expropriate some of the city streets to provide for the orderly development of the whole area, which will eventually give Toronto the seaport facilities to which it will undoubtedly be entitled with the coming of the St. Lawrence seaway.
That is a very serious problem. They should have discretion to see that this development takes full advantage of the seaport area and is not impeded in any way by either companies or other governmental agencies which may not have the same opportunity, or may have more definite interests at heart than the commission which has been designed to take care of those problems which exist in the south end of the city. We shall welcome the opportunity of having a look at each item in committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 263, to implement the convention on damage caused by foreign aircraft to third parties on the surface.
He said: This is a bill to implement the Rome convention on damage caused by foreign aircraft to third parties on the surface.
In 1933 certain nations signed at Rome a convention which set up international rules to govern the liability of air carriers for damage to persons and property on the ground. This convention was ratified by only five countries and was not effective. Since the war new developments in international civil aviation have emphasized more forcefully than ever the necessity for an international convention with regard to damage caused by aircraft to innocent third parties on the surface. It seemed desirable to the international civil aviation organization to make a fresh start on the problem and to set up, on the basis of the old Rome convention and in the light of the subsequent experience, a new convention which would ensure a just indemnity to third parties and give carriers the necessary protection against risk of liabilities so excessive as to make the cost of insurance a prohibitively heavy burden.
Though I shall not go so far as to say that the convention which is set out in the schedule to the bill is a perfect solution of the problem, I think it is a reasonable compromise of different views on legal principles and varying economic circumstances. I think in considering this legislation it ought not to be forgotten that, because the various countries concerned have different points of

view and different legal systems, an international convention is almost always the result of a compromise among their representatives.
The Rome convention was adopted at a conference held in 1952 in which Canada participated. Fifteen of the 32 countries represented at the conference signed the convention at that time; and though other countries, including the United Kingdom and Australia, have since added their signatures, only one country has ratified it. The Minister of Transport signed the convention on behalf of Canada on May 26, 1954.
The convention will come into effect when five countries have ratified it. I understand that some states are approaching the point of ratification, and I hope the convention will come into force in all countries in the world where civil aviation is developed.
The convention established a uniform measure of liability upon civil aircraft operators to any person who suffers damage on the surface when such damage, either in respect of loss of life or personal injury or in respect of property, was caused by foreign aircraft in flight or by any person or thing falling from it. It is based on the principle of objective liability; that is to say, from the moment any damage caused by a foreign aircraft in flight is sustained by a person on the ground, the carrier, that is to say the operator of the aircraft, becomes absolutely liable within the limitation specified by the convention.
The carrier can avoid this obligation only if he is able to establish (a) that the damage was a direct consequence of armed conflict or civil disturbance; (b) that he has been deprived of the use of his aircraft by act of public authority; or (c) that the damage was caused solely through the negligence or other wrongful act or omission of the person who suffers the damage or of the latter's servants or agents.	.
The limit of liability is based on the weight of the aircraft but is of such an amount that full compensation will be paid in all save very exceptional circumstances. In the case of a small aircraft weighing 1,000 kilograms or 2,200 pounds or less, the maximum liability would be 500,000 gold francs which is equal to $37,000. As will be observed from article II of the convention, the maximum liability increases progressively with the weight of the aircraft. Thus in the case of an aircraft weighing 100,000 pounds the maximum would be approximately $775,000. The liability in respect of loss of life or personal injury is limited to 500,000 gold francs or about $37,000, for each person killed or injured.
Foreign Aircraft
The carrier is entitled to the protection of these limits of liability except in the case of a deliberate act or omission done with intent to cause damage, in which case the liability is unlimited. In this way a carrier is given very significant protection in the event of an accident amounting to a catastrophe.
A further protection to the carrier is the introduction of the rule of the single forum. The convention provides that actions under its provisions may be brought only before the courts of the contracting state where the damage occurred, though by agreement claimants may take action before the courts of any other contracting state. In addition to the advantage of the single forum, the convention provides that judgments delivered in one contracting state can be executed in another contracting state without further litigation.
The convention provides for security for the carrier's liability by insurance effected in accordance with the laws of the state where the aircraft is registered. Alternative means of security are provided by cash deposit, bank guarantee, or state guarantee when the state is prepared to waive immunity for suit in respect of the guarantee.
The air transport board is satisfied that implementation of the convention by Canada, would be in the interest both of Canadian carriers and the general public. Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian Pacific Air Lines Limited, both of which are engaged in international air transport, are in agreement and have strongly recommended Canadian adherence.
Looking at the Rome convention broadly, I would say that on the one hand it provides reasonable safeguards for the injured victims on the ground in respect of damage to life and property in that they would have an uncontested claim for much if not all of the damage they might suffer from an accident caused by foreign aircraft. On the other hand the carrier is not forced to bear the heavy burden of carrying insurance against unlimited risk. Having regard to the diversity of national laws covering international air transport, there is the great advantage of having a uniform set of rules to govern liability for damage caused by foreign aircraft to third persons on the surface.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I feel a little like the pinch-hitter who appears at every game. I wonder if it would be possible for the minister to have this bill referred to committee as well. The reason I ask this is that I have looked over the debates in the other

Foreign Aircraft
place and I find that there was a great deal of confusion about the meaning of numerous sections of the bill, or at least of the schedule. Perhaps it would be much easier to go through a lengthy document of this kind in committee than it would be in the house. If that assurance is not forthcoming I shall have to go on and deal with the bill.

If I might interrupt my hon. friend I think I should say this to him, that I am not putting the legislation of the house on a take it or leave it basis. That would be far from my intention, and I would not wish hon. members to think for an instant that was the spirit in which I approached this subject. But the fact remains that, just as was said in the other place, it is not going to be possible to change one word of the convention. I think hon. members must themselves make up their minds as to whether or not the convention should be accepted as it is or whether it should be rejected.

Then, Mr. Speaker, before we go into the committee of the whole there are a few aspects in connection with this legislation which excite my mind a little.
First of all, I feel that there is a possibility in connection with this agreement that we may find our Canadian air carriers priced out of the foreign market. Now, I am not using the term "priced" in its ordinary sense; I am using it in connection with the provisions here dealing with security. It reminds me a little of the GATT agreement. I am sure I shall be accused of being out of order in referring to that subject. It is nice to enter into these agreements, but it is not nice later when one of the contracting parties says, "There is an emergency here, and we are short of foreign exchange; we cannot allow you to send your products in here". It is possible for something similar to happen under this legislation. I am referring specifically at this time to chapter III, "Security for Operator's Liability," article 15, paragraph 4:
Instead of insurance, any of the following securities shall be deemed satisfactory if the security conforms to article 17.
Paragraph 3 and the three subparagraphs of paragraph 4 refer to the accepting of satisfactory insurance. Paragraph 3 states:
. . . the state overflown may refuse to accept as satisfactory insurance effected by an insurer who is not authorized for that purpose in a contracting state.

Paragraph 4 says that the securities provided in each case
. . . shall be deemed satisfactory if the security conforms to article 17:
(a) a cash deposit in a depository maintained by the contracting state where the aircraft is registered or with a bank authorized to act as a depository by that state;
Which paragraph?

Subparagraph (a) of paragraph 4. It would appear to me that subparagraphs (b) and (c), although the terms are slightly different in each case, provide the discretionary power for the contracting party to approve or not to approve of the type of securities provided. As I see it, if Trans-Canada Air Lines should be working under a bilateral agreement with any number of parties to this agreement, and if it should be determined at any time by one of those contracting parties that they did not like the services provided by the Canadian air line, I see nothing to prevent them from ordering a type of security which would have the effect of placing an embargo on our air services entering their country. That would appear to be one serious problem which confronts us here.
The minister might be able as well to give us some explanation as to the meaning of the amounts arrived at here, on the basis of dollars. I am not a monetary expert. I understand that the minister referred to the amount of 500,000 gold francs, and perhaps he can explain whether they are any different from the other type of francs used in France today.
Quite different.

We might have some explanation as to that, because if they are not, then obviously the liability here might amount to 10 cents, as far as we are concerned. If there is some stability to that type of currency which is provided in this international agreement, then I believe that the limits provided here exceed the minimum financial limits required by our own air transport board in connection with domestic air operations.
A third problem which confronts us is in connection with the ability of the contracting party to be cleared of any liability in connection with civil insurrection-I believe that is the term-in the country involved. I am wondering what would be the effect if, for instance, in a foreign country there was some type of civil uprising, someone planted a bomb in that case in a Trans-Canada Air Lines plane-this is not fantasy, by the way- and as the result of an explosion over a third country we found some question of liability.

Perhaps I have used the wrong air line. If it happened to be a foreign air line which was flying into Canada, say over Brampton, and some explosion of that nature occurred, is it possible under this legislation that complete immunity would be obtained because the accident was the direct result of, say, some civil problem arising in another state?
I also notice that there is for a period of time a continuing responsibility on the owner of an aircraft after the sale of the aircraft. This factor might have a distressing effect in connection with a Canadian operator of an aircraft. I know that under our insurance coverage it is provided-and I suppose the situation is the same in nearly all jurisdictions -that your car insurance continues to cover you after the sale of your automobile and, I think, for a period when you acquire a new one; but in this type of liability in which the owner may actually part with possession and legal ownership it is questionable whether there should be a continuing responsibility of this kind.
The minister has indicated that this agreement has the full approval of both Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I feel some regret that neither of those companies, as I understand it, was invited to attend or to have any representative along with the representatives of the air transport board or the Department of Transport when negotiating this agreement. After all, they are certainly the two major parties in the country which are involved in connection with this legislation. I know that the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines has indicated that this legislation fills the bill so far as they are concerned, and that he feels satisfied with it. At the same time I feel that representatives of both these operating companies could easily have been included in the group which negotiated this agreement.
I am a little bit surprised as well that the minister has not been able to indicate the acceptance of this legislation by any great number of countries. Of course we are especially interested in the situation with regard to the United States. I understand that as yet there is no indication that the United States is even close to accepting this legislation. Without their acceptance of it I would think that one of our major problems in connection with air transport in this country-because several of their companies have certain rights in and through Canada-will be left uncovered. If the minister could give us any assurance that they are expected shortly to enter into this agreement I think a major problem would be overcome.
Foreign Aircraft
There is only one other matter to which I wish to refer. In connection with liability I have mentioned that the convention apparently provides limits which, so far as I am aware, exceed some of the limits set by our own air transport board. It also provides, of course, that where negligence is proved there is no limitation whatsoever. I wonder whether the provisions dealing with security are adequate to take care of the situation involving the negligent operation of an aircraft. After all, if there is an accident in which an aircraft of foreign registry is involved in Canada, it is quite possible that the only asset which will be available for execution will be the damaged aircraft itself after the minimum insurance coverage has been paid.
To a great extent this is a problem of property and civil rights, and in dealing with a problem of this kind it is a question whether the federal government should not go a step further and ensure that security be available to cover all losses, not just losses occasioned where no negligence is proved. It would appear that the legal rule of res ipsa loquitur has been used here. That would appear to solve only one part of the problem. The other part perhaps should have been taken care of through the same system.

speechtext: The schedule is one clause but if it is agreeable to the committee we can call the schedule, for purposes of discussion, chapter by chapter. Chapter I is "Principles of Liability".

May I ask the minister whether Canada would be bound by this

Foreign Aircraft
agreement as soon as five countries have subscribed to it, notwithstanding the fact that the other country involved in an accident was not a party to the agreement?
My understanding of that matter is that although Canada would be bound, it would be only in respect of the contracting states.

That is what I want to
know. It would only be countries-
And who had also ratified.
-who had ratified. If Canada ratified we would then be liable when their aircraft were here and they would be liable if our aircraft were there, but not otherwise.
That is so.

At the end of
the last sentence of the first paragraph there are the words, "in conformity with existing air traffic regulations". Would the minister advise us if all contracting parties to this agreement have common air traffic regulations, or are there different aircraft regulations in each of the contracting countries?

My information is that they are, of course, matters of separate regulation in each country. Just as Canada has the right to determine its air traffic rules, so would the other contracting states; but, as Mr. Matthews has informed me, there is a good deal of uniformity as between the various sets of regulations.
Does that mean that in each case it would be the courts of the individual country which would interpret the air regulations of that country?

I think the hon. member is losing sight of the fact that as a result of the convention the mere fact that the damage is caused by a foreign aircraft to a third person on the surface makes it unnecessary to go into the question of whether it was following the rules or was not following them. In other words, it is deemed to be liable and it can only escape liability under the condition set forth in article 5, which reads:
Any person who would otherwise be liable under the provisions of this convention shall not be liable if the damage is the direct consequence of armed conflict or civil disturbance, or if such person has been deprived of the use of the aircraft by act of public authority.
In other words, if an engine drops off and causes damage you do not have to prove negligence. You merely have to prove the fact of the damage.

The minister might enlighten us in connection with the

other instance, where there is negligence to be proven and where there is going to be unlimited liability. Will that not be according to the particular regulation and in the country's courts?

No. The point I was trying to make was that it is not necessary to prove negligence. All that is necessary is to prove damage. As the hon. member will notice in reading the convention, if the damage occurs in the province of Ontario, let us say, the person suffering the damage sues in the courts of the province of Ontario and he does not have to prove that the accident was due to negligence. He merely proves the fact of the damage. That obviously is the advantage of the convention, which is counterbalanced, I think hon. members will agree, by the fact that there is a limitation of liability. If we were to have no convention, as I understand the situation, negligence would have to be proved and there is no limitation on liability at the present time, with the result that it might be possible to get a judgment but it might not be possible to enforce it. The effect of the convention is, first of all, to eliminate the necessity of proving negligence, to establish the place where the suit must be brought, and to provide a fund, if you like, or security upon which the judgment can be realized by a simple process.
Perhaps we are talking at cross-purposes. Do I not understand that this does not limit liability where negligence can be proven?

I am afraid the hon. member is misinterpreting the sense of the convention. Once the convention becomes effective, saving acts of deliberate damage to which I referred earlier, whether or not negligence is proven the liability is limited in accordance with the statement to which the hon. member alluded a moment ago. Perhaps I had better deal later with the question of the gold francs.

Chapter I, article 1, subsection 2, says that an aircraft is considered to be in flight from the moment when power is applied for the purpose of actual take-off until the moment when the landing run ends. Do I understand from this that taxiing into position at the start of a flight and taxiing to the unloading place do not enter into the question of liability here in case there is an accident during that particular operation? In other words, how do you determine when the actual take-off occurs and the landing run ends?

I think the convention is pretty clear on that subject. The aircraft is considered to be in flight from the moment when power is applied for the purpose of actual take-off until the moment when the landing run ends. As we are talking about aircraft and not craft lighter than air I think it is perfectly obvious that the convention does not apply during the so-called taxiing operation. I should like to remind the hon. member that this does not concern damage to people in the aircraft. It is damage to people on the surface.
People have been injured when airplanes have been taxiing into position or when the engines have been started, and so on, and I was wondering why that was not mentioned.
If a four-motor American Air Lines plane was warming up its motors at Malton airport and one of the propellers flew off and killed somebody, that person would not be covered under the convention?
I do not think the convention applies in that case.
Does the minister know of any particular reason for that?
Not having participated in the 1952 negotiations I am unable to answer that question.

Do I understand that under article 2 there is this continuing liability to which I referred previously, and that the owner may have parted with legal title and yet be considered responsible under the convention?

I think the answer to that is yes. If I may reply at this moment to what the hon. member said during the debate on second reading, I should like to draw his attention to the provision of subparagraph 4 of article 11 which shows what is the meaning of a gold franc. I am sure if he reads that clause carefully he will find that inasmuch as the gold franc is tied to a certain quantity of gold it can hardly be expected to fluctuate as violently as he implied a little earlier. I did say that 500,000 francs were the equivalent of $37,000, and by my arithmetic that would be 7-4 cents for a gold franc.
I was going to say that at the price the government pays for gold it would never change. Is there any particular reason-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: At six o'clock we were discussing chapter II of the schedule.

Can the
minister give us any idea why the 14-day period was selected for the continuing liability?
To which clause is the hon. member referring?
That is article 3.
I am looking at article 15 because I understand that chapters I and II had been adopted.

speechtext: Chapter III starts on page 6.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I do not think
there is any wish on the part of the committee to limit discussion, so perhaps we might revert to that article for the moment.

I think I could answer my hon. friend by saying that we do not know why the period of 14 days to which he has referred was selected. Evidently that was the agreement in 1952, and I do not think it has any particular significance.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall we pass on now to chapter II?

Foreign Aircraft

No, Mr. Chairman. Article 5 on page 3 puzzles me a bit. If the owner of an aircraft is deprived of its use by the act of a public authority, whose responsibility is it? As an example, assume that an agency of the United States government seizes an American Air Lines plane flying into Malton to transport refugees, or whatever you want to call them. Is there any liability on that party then under this convention?

If I understand the hypothetical case to which my hon. friend refers, if the United States government deprives one of its citizens of the use of his aircraft and then flies it over Canada, I take it that under article 5 the owner of the aircraft is relieved from liability under the convention because he has not the control of the aircraft, as this public authority has taken it away from him.

Would the
state then become the operator and also be liable?
I notice that in another section of the bill, in defining the meaning of the word "person", it goes so far as to cover the state. If my friend looks at article 30 he will see that.

The only point in connection with that, Mr. Chairman, is that I think the two terms used have been "owner" and "operator" and not "person" up to this point. I may be wrong. No, "person" is used; that is quite right.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Anything further on chapter I?

Yes, article 7, which I have read along with article 13 on page 6, which is part of chapter II. Is it the intention here that both operators of the aircraft which subsequently injures a third party will be liable through the insurance fund or otherwise to the full extent of the coverage?
Yes, that is correct.
Is that not an unusual situation? Ordinarily when third parties are involved is it not usual that the liability is limited to one stipulated amount?

I will not generalize, but as I understand the convention each aircraft will be liable up to the full limit that is mentioned in the convention.
Mr. Hamilton (York West)-: In other words this would be almost what you would term a double indemnity clause. If T.C.A. were involved in an accident over foreign territory
[The Deputy Chairman.]
and on a negligence basis were only responsible to the extent of 25 per cent, they would still have to pay the total amount out of this insurance fund?
That is the limit of the liability of each of them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Anything further on chapter I? Shall we go to chapter II, "Extent of Liability?"

The minister spent a considerable time explaining to me the gold franc system, and the Minister of Finance has assisted me at various times as well. Is there no way this amount can be tied to a current price? The minister was able to explain that the limit of liability on a light aircraft amounted to about $37,000. I assume that was based on the present price of gold. Would it not be true, notwithstanding the formula used, that if tomorrow the United States decided $25 per ounce was going to be the price paid for gold, this formula would leave us paying out to an aggrieved party possibly only three-fifths of the amount the minister has mentioned. Is that not something that could take place?

As I understand it, Mr. Chairman, the significance of article 11, particularly the fourth paragraph, is that the measure of damage is expressed in gold francs and the gold franc is not expressed in currency but is converted into 65J milligrammes of gold of millesimal fineness 900. I take it that if there is fluctuation you have always to go back to what is the worth of 65J milligrammes of gold of that particular fineness. I would find it difficult, offhand, to suggest some other measure that would remain constant that would be better than this.

Under article 12, which is still in chapter II, there are paragraphs 1 and 2. They seem to leave unlimited liability in a case of wilful damage. Does that still envisage that the minimum amount under the convention insurance fund will be payable notwithstanding what the final judgment might be?

I think it is obvious that the purpose of this section is to remove the limitation on liability that we have been discussing. At the same time I do not suppose that the insurance is going to be for an unlimited amount. I take it that the insurance that would be required would be up to a certain limit. I think the provisions are stated further on. I do not think you could expect to recover more than the limits of the insurance.

Does the
minister understand that the same thing would take place as takes place in connection with automobile insurance? When $20,000 is covered out of a claim amounting to $40,000, does this paragraph contemplate that $20,000 must be paid, namely that the minimum requirement must be paid?
Yes.

From reading article 14 it would appear that in dealing with personal and property damage there has been a division of the amount available for the satisfaction of a claim. It would seem that it is divided into two parts, 50 per cent for personal loss and 50 per cent for property damage, with the overriding feature that in respect of property damage if the 50 per cent more than covers the property damage claim the balance available would go toward the payment of personal injury claims.
I would gather the effect might be this, that there might be claims in connection with personal injury amounting to $50,000, in which four or five persons would be involved, and that there might be only $25,000 involved in property damage suffered by different persons. They might get all their money, whereas those making claims for personal injuries might receive only a small percentage of those claims. Would that be the result, under the wording of this article?

My understanding is that this article applies only in a case where the amount of the claims exceeds the amount of the security. My understanding of the convention is that it provides that the first half shall be divisible among claimants in respect of bodily injury or loss of life. So far as the other half is concerned, it would be available not only to those claims in respect of damage to property but also to the first group so far as their claims remained unsatisfied out of the first half.

But does not this arbitrary division have the effect of separating the arrangement so that in one section we might have a situation where a total claim was paid out, 100 cents on the dollar, whereas in the other section it would be paid out to the extent of only 10 cents on the dollar?

No, I do not think so. I will not challenge the last figure, because I do not think it is relevant. But the position must be that the claims exceed the amount available for distribution. The point is that one-half goes to the claimants in respect of bodily injury or loss of life. The other half is divided up among the same group of claimants and the claimants in respect of property.
Foreign Aircraft
So far as I can see it is impossible that any group should receive payment in full. In fact,
I think if the hon. member would carefully examine the article in the convention he would find that it gives a sort of priority to those who have claims for bodily injury or loss of life.

I may be slow in understanding this, but if there is one group of people with personal injury claims amounting to $100,000 on one side and $25,000 property damage on the other, and there is a policy for $150,000-
You have too much money.

-and we
divide it under this system, I think you will find that the property damage people are getting all their claims, while the personal damage people are getting only a dividend on their claims. Is it possible that that might happen under this article?

In the figures my hon. friend just gave as to the amount of claims he started off on the premise that the claims were less than the amount available for distribution. Of course on that basis everybody would be paid in full. But if there is only $100,000, and let us say claims for personal injury of $75,000 and claims for property damage of $75,000, those who have the claims of $75,000 for bodily injury will receive half the $100,000, or $50,000. That leaves claimants of $25,000 for bodily injury, plus claimants of $75,000 for property damage to divide up the remaining $50,000. I think my hon. friend will realize that the claims in respect of bodily injury will receive another $12,500 and those in respect of property damage will receive $37,500. So that the claimants for bodily injury will be receiving $62,500 while the others would receive $37,500. I hope my arithmetic is right, and I think it is. But the principle is quite clear, according to the article in the convention.
Would it not be fairer if the whole amount were pooled and a proportionate dividend paid to all, pro rata?

Offhand I must say that I think the individual ought to be compensated in respect of bodily injury or loss of life before compensation is given for property damage. That may be a matter of opinion, but it was certainly the opinion of those who drew the convention.

But you do not
compensate him first. You just divide the fund; is that not right?

Foreign Aircraft
I do not think I can add much to what I have said.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Then we will pass on to chapter III, which deals with security for operator's liability.

This is the chapter dealing with the requirements of contracting nations in connection with insurance coverage requirements and/or the cash requirements and bank guarantees, or otherwise required to be filed covering the responsibilities of the various parties.
In connection with the interpretation of these articles-and I do not wish to refer to any one in particular-is it not possible for a contracting party to refuse any of the types of security mentioned here, as being unsatisfactory to it?

Mr. Chairman, I think it might be said that under the convention there might be a dispute as to the sufficiency of insurance. There are provisions under which a contracting state may dispute an insurance payment. There is provision for discussion as to the insurance and the settlement of the dispute. I think paragraph 7(a) enables a state overflown to request additional evidence of financial responsibility. But, unfortunately, perhaps this is somewhat reduced in efficacy by paragraph 7(b) which provides that in the event of a dispute between states as to financial responsibility the insurance or guarantee shall continue valid until the dispute has been settled by an arbitral tribunal. I admit that is not a very satisfactory outcome, but on the other hand I do not think that anybody would be particularly interested in maintaining insurance that really was not effective because after all, as my hon. friend knows, if the insurer is not going to pay at the appropriate time the insured in this particular case is going to have to provide the moneys.

In chapter IV, provision is made for the commencement of an action within a certain length of time. Further down in the chapter reference is made to the possible revision of the whole action by the court of the other contracting party. Some provision should be made that would set out when the judgment will be final, rather than allowing it to be reviewed by the courts of the other contracting party. Look at article 19 of chapter IV and read article 20, paragraph 5. Article 19 provides for the commencement of the action and paragraph 5 apparently provides for a complete review.

I think that refers only to the execution of the judgment. As I understand it, article 19 says that the time for the

bringing of the action is six months, but the paragraph to which my hon. friend has just referred, as I understand it, deals with the execution of the judgment; that is to say, after the facts have been determined and the operator of the aircraft found liable.

In connection with chapter IV, article 20, paragraph 5, under the rules of which court of competent jurisdiction would the proceedings dealing with the reopening of the proceedings be taken? What might be considered as a fair service of notice under the rules of one court might not be satisfactory service under the rules of the other court. I can see this situation arising. The court where the execution is issued might be a foreign court, and it might refer to proceedings taken in the court where the judgment was obtained as not giving proper notice to the defendant. The court where the notice was given might consider that it was quite proper notice. Is there any indication here as to which rules will be followed, the rules of the court where the execution was issued or the rules of the court where the judgment was obtained?

I take it, of course, from what was said earlier in the discussion that the judgment is obtained in the state in which the accident occurred. I cited this afternoon as an example that if the damage were suffered in the province of Ontario, the action would be brought in the province of Ontario and judgment rendered. But I do not believe it would follow that the judgment of the Ontario court is necessarily going to be executed in, let us say, the place where the operator of the aircraft has his principal establishment. It might be found convenient to take proceedings for execution in the state of New York; and I take it that the rules which are set forth in paragraph 5 would be determined by the court in which the judgment creditor attempted to enforce execution of his judgment.
I take it my hon. friend would feel that it was not unfair that the court which was being asked to order execution of some foreign judgment might reasonably say, "Was the defendant given a fair and adequate opportunity to defend his interests?" I am quite sure my hon. friend would not wish to find that his client, for example, had been condemned by a court of some other country on what seemed to him to be totally insufficient motives. I think he would like to feel that his client would be protected at the crucial moment when execution was asked for, and to know that the court would make certain that adequate notice of the action was given originally.

Without having practised before the courts I must say that it does seem to me that in a general sense these provisions are intended to ensure that the person being asked to pay will receive justice.

I was thinking more of protection for our own operators in connection with obtaining execution of their judgments in a foreign country. Obviously, under this paragraph, it is quite definite that the merits of the case cannot be reopened, but the rules of the court dealing with service may be entirely different in country X than they are in the province of Ontario. I go further and say that under paragraph 7 I find that we are also subject to the whims and fancies of the public policy of the state in which the execution is requested. Country X may be down in South America, so far as I am concerned, and what may be public policy there from day to day may materially affect our air operators' opportunity of collecting a judgment.
Surely not of collecting, but of having to pay, is it not?
Well, I would say it is the ability to collect through the process of issuing execution under these paragraphs.

I think my hon. friend is forgetting that the people who are benefiting through this convention so far as these claims are concerned are third persons on the surface. The case that he has just referred to, I take it, is that of a resident of some foreign country in Central or South America who may obtain in the courts there a judgment against, let us say, Trans-Canada Air Lines, and I suppose that if he could enforce that judgment against property down there that would be the Trans-Canada Air Lines' misfortune. If it considered it did not receive adequate notice, the judgment would not be enforceable in the courts of Ontario, let us say, unless the conditions set forth in paragraph 5 were realized.

I may have used a wrong example. Perhaps I should have said a citizen of Ontario having obtained a judgment in Ontario and attempting to force execution in country X is subject, as I see it here and if I understand the minister's interpretation of the rules of court, to the rules of court in foreign country X so far as the efficacy of service is concerned and subject to the whims and fancies, if I may use that term, of public policy of that state. Is that right?

I think so, yes. But I should like to point out to my hon. friend that that
Foreign Aircraft
is the situation now. Regardless of the convention, if the aircraft is registered in some foreign republic and if an individual wishes now to enforce a claim for damages, he obtains a judgment from the Ontario court. If there is something within the jurisdiction of the Ontario court on which he can obtain execution, well and good. If he cannot, he knows that he has to go to the republic and in the courts there run his chances of being able to exemplify and execute a foreign judgment. I am sure the hon. member has tried to execute foreign judgments in Canada, and I am quite sure he realizes it is not a simple process.
This convention does not add anything to the person's rights?
I think not.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES

subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES
speechtext:
I welcome anything that will be of assistance to those who are suffering from this handicap, and the fact that the age is lowered from 21 to 18 years is a step in the right direction. Personally I feel-and I should like to hear the minister's comments on this matter.-that if the age were still further lowered to, say, 16, when other assistance in the nature of family allowances ceases, that money could be well used' at a time when it was necessary for the education of these people who have this affliction. I think education for these people at an early age is a very important thing and that such special assistance, even lowering the age two years more, would enable them to obtain further education and fit them to carry on their lives under their handicap.
I received, as I suppose every other member of the house did, sometime about February, a brief from the Canadian council of the blind and the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. I am also very much aware of the splendid work being done by voluntary organizations in this line, and I would also mention the fact that medical science is doing a great deal in the way of prevention of this disability. But I note that the Canadian national council of the blind bring forth three recommendations; they comment on these, and at the finish of their brief they summarize these recommendations.
The first recommendation-and this was
made before the minister introduced his legislation-was that the Blind Persons Act be amended, substituting age 18 years for the present 21 years for recipients of the blindness allowance. So the present resolution covers the first recommendation of the Canadian council of the blind.
The second recommendation was that the means test ceiling provided in the Blind Persons Act be raised to statutory minimum levels for single and married persons now applicable in the Canadian Income Tax Act.
The third recommendation was that a special guiding allowance of at least $10 per month be provided by the government of Canada, free from the means test, to all blind persons from the age of 18 years for life.
In their general comment-and these figures are interesting, because I think figures produced by the organization are authentic- they point out that elimination of the means test on the present blindness allowance would affect only some 3,800 persons in the age

group 21 to 69 who are not now on the allowance, plus those who are on the allowance but tor whom the amount has been reduced more or less because of income in excess of the present ceiling. The explanations they make are interesting. They estimate that the elimination of the means test would cost approximately $2 million, and they say further:
Hence, the elimination of the means test would benefit only a few of the 8,000 presently on blindness allowance and none of the 7,500 on old age security.
Then they give revised recommendations. Again the first is that the age reduction from 21 to 18 would add approximately 290 to those on blindness allowance and would cost about $139,200 per annum. That is covered by the resolution. The second is that the increased ceiling recommended would add approximately 500 and would cost $240,000. The third is that a guiding allowance free from the means test would cover approximately 19,000 and would cost $2,280,000. So the estimated cost of the three recommendations made by the Canadian national council of the blind would amount to approximately $2,500,000 per annum. The first recommendation brought in by the minister today is going to cost $139,200.
They also pointed out that the principle endorsed by the world council for the welfare of the blind involves the payment of maintenance allowance to the less capable blind, subject to a more or less generous means test and a guiding allowance.
We welcome the resolution brought in by the minister. We think it is a good resolution. I am sure every person in the chamber will approve this assistance to these handicapped people. Yet one must recognize two other recommendations made by the Canadian council of the blind. In any future legislation I think we should proceed as far as we can toward implementing these recommendations from such a responsible body.
As I said, I welcome the additional amount that is being paid. I think it is a step in the right direction. But I think that the whole committee will feel that in future legislation we should proceed as far as possible toward implementing those recommendations.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am going to be brief because I think there is unanimity in the committee in support of the proposals contained in this resolution. I join with the hon. member in saying that I think the age limit should have been lower than it is. I agree with him that
Blind Persons Act
when family allowance ceases the blind pension should begin. That would be at the age of 16. However, we have gone about this particular piece of social security legislation bit by bit and step by step.
I was here, of course, when the first blind pension plan was introduced. I had been greatly interested in the problems of the blind for many years. In fact at one time I had the honour of being honorary president of an organization in my own province and I was able to meet the blind people at that time, to understand their problems, and to realize how essential it was that something constructive should be done for them.
I quite agree that, after all, the education of the blind is of paramount importance. We have schools for them in various places, more particularly in the province of Ontario. One thing I should like to see is the adoption of a plan whereby the federal government might assist the provinces in building schools for perhaps two or more provinces. I should like to see one for the three prairie provinces so the children would not be obliged to go so far afield and be away from their parents for such long periods of time.
Many of the blind people, given the opportunity, are able partly to earn their own living. They are severely handicapped, hence can rarely make an income which is sufficient to meet all their needs. But given the opportunity they can at least partially provide for themselves. That is one of the reasons that I should like to see the ceiling on the earnings they may get from their labour, whatever it may be, increased considerably. I think the suggestion of the institute is reasonable, namely that the ceiling should be raised to the income tax minimum in the cases of single and married people.
But while I am of that opinion, I am much more interested in seeing the eligibility age reduced. I should like to see it reduced as soon as possible to the age of 16. As a matter of fact I should be inclined to go lower than 16, in order to help provide for the education of the child at an early age. After all, the parents assume an obligation and often a tremendous burden in caring for a blind child. Then too, the request for some allowance for a guide is, in my opinion, reasonable and fair.
While we are extending our social security system in various directions I think there is no more worthy cause than the extension of the system to those who are handicapped by loss of sight. It is true, I am happy to say, that modern medical science, as has already been pointed out, is doing much to remove

Blind Persons Act
blindness from our midst. Often sight can be restored. If the child is taken in hand soon after birth, often the threat of blindness can be removed by physicians. That consideration, of course, brings me to the hardy chestnut of our movement, namely that the provision of medical aid on a national basis is something that should round out our social security system. It would be of assistance in cases of this sort, where medical attention would be immediately available, and blindness sometimes would be prevented by speedy action by qualified physicians.
I do not think there is much I can add, except to say that we are and always have been wholeheartedly in support of this type of legislation. Speaking personally, I may say that I have always been exceedingly glad to support in this chamber any proposal which would assist this group of people in any and every way possible. I am happy indeed that this measure has been introduced. I hope that in another year at most we shall see amendments introduced designed to remove the ceiling or to raise the ceiling and reduce the age limit progressively, perhaps the next time, as requested to 16. I should like to go beyond that point and see the next step the reduction of the age below 16, before family allowance ceases.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this stage I would not think it necessary to speak at any length with regard to this resolution. However, I can say that we are grateful that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has seen fit to propose to the House of Commons a measure which will do the two things that are outlined in the resolution, namely reduce from 21 to 18 years the age at which blind persons become eligible for assistance, and increase the maximum annual incomes allowed to recipients.
At this stage we do not know how much the increase will be in annual income, but we are certainly in favour of both these things that are specifically mentioned in the resolution. We should like the minister to know that we would support a considerable increase in the ceiling on annual income allowed to blind persons because, as has already been pointed out, these people are carrying on under great handicaps. They require a much higher income than do ordinary persons, in order that they may do the things they are obliged to do. The cost of their training is much greater, the cost of assistance to get around is much greater, and all that sort of thing.
I am quite sure we are not telling the minister anything he does not already know. We are hopeful that he will take into full consideration the requests that have been

made by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, in which I believe they mentioned the necessity for granting some allowance to blind persons in order to help them pay for guides where it is necessary to have guides. I do not know anything at all about the cost of a guide. I have not the slightest idea of what it costs to obtain and to maintain a seeing-eye dog or even to obtain the services of a human guide where it is necessary. However, the cost must be considerable. I would think that is nothing more than reasonable that we should give careful consideration to the requests that have been made that these people be given a certain allowance each year for guide purposes.
We would prefer to wait until the measure comes before us to debate the matter at any length, and so we reserve our criticism until we come to second reading of the bill. Suffice it to say at this time that we are very happy to see progress being made in the right direction, and we do hope the minister has gone as far as it is possible for him to induce his colleagues to go along with him at this time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on the resolution. I have a great deal of sympathy for those who do not have their sight, and I believe it comes closer home to me than to most members of the House of Commons because of the fact that a daughter of mine was thrown from her horse some years ago, landed on her head and as a result of that accident became blind.
I know what a blind person has to go through in this life. I have had dealings not only with one blind person but with a great number, and. may I say they do not want sympathy. They want to be able to work on their own and do things themselves. That is one way the Canadian National Institute for the Blind has done a lot for them. They send teachers and instructors to the blind people if the blind people want them. These teachers and instructors have taught them to read braille. They have taught them to use typewriters and other machines that even the minister or I, having our sight, perhaps could not handle. They have taught them to do many things. They have taught them to earn their own living.
But these blind men and women who have gone out to earn their living have found that they cannot get the pension owing to the fact that their earnings are too great. At the same time it costs a blind person more money to live than it does the man working at the next machine, because the blind person has to have someone guide him to the bus and to the plant where he is

working. He has to be picked up again and taken home. In the home he has to be instructed to a certain extent, although not very much, in this and that, and shown where certain things are.
During the years the Canadian National Institute for the Blind has been in operation-and I speak particularly of the Peterborough branch with which I have had a lot to do-it has had to supplement the incomes of blind people in order that they might have fuel in their homes in the wintertime, proper clothing and medical attention and other little things they could not get on the blind pension or even when working and living at home. Most of these blind people are very intelligent. This is partly because of the fact that the Canadian National Institute for the Blind has supplied them with what are known as talking books. These are volumes of records on literature, history and geography. They have the Reader's Digest and the Bible in so many volumes, and the blind people can learn things by playing the records in these talking books. This is something else these people have to have in order to get along, but these books cost money.
There are many other things they have to have. The hon. member who just spoke mentioned seeing-eye dogs. Personally I am not very keen on blind people having seeing-eye dogs owing to the fact that they depend on the seeing-eye dog instead of depending on themselves. I think they lose something by having a seeing-eye dog, though these dogs will take them wherever they wish to go.
There is not much more I wish to say. In my opinion the lowering of the pensionable age from 21 to 18 is not good enough. It should be lowered to at least 16, as the hon. member for Lanark and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned, in order to pick up where the family allowance leaves off. There is a gap there of two years during which the parent has to look after the blind child. It is not fair. It means they have to deprive themselves and their other children, if they have any, of many necessities of life in order to look after the one child who needs extra attention. I hope that the ceiling on allowable income will be high enough so these people will not have to deprive themselves of things they have had to deprive themselves of in the past.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I regret that the minister did not choose to introduce this resolution with any remarks. I know he is waiting for us to conclude. However, I am pleased to see so much interest taken in the resolution at this time. I wonder whether
Blind Persons Act
the minister is so keenly aware of the situation, when the government is unable to see its way clear to give our blind people a dollar more out of every $10,000 of our national production. If we granted all the amendments to the act they asked for in their brief it would, as the hon. member for Lanark pointed out, cost $2 million, a little below 1 per cent of 1 per cent of our national production. I think their brief was like that presented to the government by the returned men of Canada. It was deliberately designed with the hope that it would appear so reasonable to the government that the government would not be able to find an argument as to why their requests should not be completely met.
I do not think the brief really represents what the members of the institute feel they should have. So far the only amendment about which we know anything definitely is that lowering the age of eligibility to 18. According to the brief that will cost the government only $139,200 a year. If I were a minister offering such a great social reform I would also hesitate to speak on the introduction of the resolution. After all, it would amount to only a relatively minor amendment.
In looking over the act I notice that this is another case where the federal government embarks on something in co-operation with the provincial governments on the basis of sharing the cost. I realize that possibly this is an invasion of provincial rights. However, I see no reason why this government has to limit itself to paying only 75 per cent of the cost of this pension. In these days we are particularly concerned about how we can rearrange the incomes of our lower levels of government. I think relief to some extent might be offered to the provincial governments if the federal government were to accept 100 per cent of the cost of blind pensions, just as they did in the case of pensions for our senior citizens over 70.
The leader of the group to which I belong pleaded with the minister to lower the eligible age for pension even more than the minister has offered. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar asked that the age be lowered to at least 16, and I was very happy to hear him use the words "at least".
I think the approach of the group to which I belong would be this. When such a tragedy happens to a family I think all of us in the community should say, not that we will shoulder the burden of this family-because no one who has a blind member of the family will ever admit it is a burden-but we should say we will shoulder the extra responsibility that you have as a result of having a member of your family who has the misfortune to be

Blind Persons Act
blind. I do not see why there should be any age limit to a blind pension paid on behalf of society as a whole, because if we say that a blind person must first reach the age of 18 to receive a pension, that person has already passed the age when a heavy outlay of money has to be made on his behalf.
Blind people like to feel that they also have a contribution to make to society and to the community in which they live. Before they can make that contribution they need training, the cost of which is away beyond the cost of an ordinary education. I feel, for that reason alone, that this pension should be payable at whatever age blindness occurs. I feel also that in many cases blind persons would have been able to regain their vision if an adequate income had been made available at an early age.
Another matter I wish to emphasize is that it seems to be taken for granted that we should pay no more in allowances to blind persons than we pay to old age pensioners. I was very happy to hear the hon. member for Peterborough place emphasis on the fact that a blind person has added expense. I believe we ought to get away from this idea of a $40 maximum for all those who receive pensions. If $40 is a suitable amount for old age pensioners, then certainly meeting the request of these national associations and allowing blind persons an extra $10 per month would not be out of the way. Even with $50 per month they would actually be receiving a great deal less than they need.
I notice the resolution mentions the maximum permissible income. We have no information as yet on what is proposed. I should like to see the legislation state that the means test will be removed altogether. I feel that the cost of administering such a means test must consume a considerable portion of the money that is saved by having such a test. This means test discourages the building up of self-respect in these people. I think they would like to find useful employment, and having a means test at all is merely discouraging these people from getting the training necessary to earn their own livelihood.
In reading the act I noticed regulations concerning the disposal of assets in order to qualify under the means test. We have gone through the mill in that respect with old age pensions. We have seen how the means test used to encourage people to illegally dispose of their assets in order to take advantage of the old age pension. I believe the Canadian people would be happy to hear the minister state that this government, in amending this act, had agreed to eliminate this means test.
In looking at the permissible income, I hope the minister will take a more liberal

attitude toward raising the ceiling than was taken when we amended the war veterans legislation. I see that the permissible income ceiling for single people is now $840 per annum. Ordinary taxpayers in Canada do not pay any income tax on the first $1,000. It is considered that one needs at least $1,000 in order to exist. I do not see why, if we are not willing to abolish the means test, we should not at least allow blind people the minimum exemption that is allowed by the Income Tax Act.
I have noticed other discrepancies which I hope to see removed when I see the bill. The maximum income allowed a single person is set at $840. Then we come to an unmarried person with one dependent child, and we see that the maximum permissible income is $1,040. This means that there is an allowance of only $200 for the care of one child for a year. I should like the minister to indicate that he is prepared to allow much more under the amendment. I feel that the allowance for one child should be at least $500 per year, because it costs even normal people that much to sustain one child for a year.
Then the maximum permissible income for a married person is set at $1,320. Again there is an increase of $480 per year over the amount allowed a single person. Surely blind people should not be asked to live on $40 per month, yet that is what we are doing when we say that single people will be allowed to have an income of $840 and married people an income of $1,320. When both the husband and wife are blind, we place a ceiling on their income of $1,440 per year or $120 per month. This $120 per month is only $10 per month more than a married couple on old age pension receive in some parts of the dominion. When both the husband and wife are blind, surely it is unreasonable for us to say that they have to get by on $120 per month.
There are not many blind people in Canada. I do not think anyone in this house will take part in this debate because of what the blind people may do at the next election. Throughout Canada there are only slightly more than 8,000 persons in receipt of assistance under the Blind Persons Act, and the total expenditures by this government under that act amount to less than $3 million a year. I feel that if the government had decided to grant all the requests of the Canadian council of the blind and the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, the Canadian people might have said, "We have a liberal government in deed as well as in name". I do not think any opposition would have been registered from any section of the house had

the government seen fit to spend that extra $2 million a year instead of a miserable $139,000.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the risk of repetition I feel impelled to support the proposals made by several hon. members. Before the minister speaks I would hope he might reconsider the suggestion he now makes, so the age limit may be reduced to 16 years.
I have listened with interest on many occasions to appeals made on behalf of the blind and of others who, as the hon. member who has just spoken said, make up a small minority of those people in our country who sometimes, under our democratic system, are almost forgotten. I have not had the same experience as my hon. friend and colleague from Peterborough. Many of us who know him well realize how close he is to this problem.
I feel impelled, however, to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Lanark, who has given serious study to this and other welfare problems. I would support, too, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar who has described explicitly the present situation. I shall not take the time of the committee to repeat what has been said. As was pointed out so well by the hon. member for Peterborough, the blind persons in this country do not want sob stories on their behalf; they do not want sympathy; they want assistance.
It is clear that from their infancy blind persons place heavy obligations upon their families. As parents and perhaps as grandparents some of us know what it means to protect children who may run out on the streets, and how much greater the obligation must be when the children are blind. It has been difficult enough to watch my progeny, even when they can see.
I cannot help thinking that we overlook the seriousness of the problem. There has been agreement in the house to give old age pensions even to many who do not need it. Then we have given pensions to others who may have wasted what they received, and we have been reluctant and hesitant-I think sometimes because they do not have many votes-to give pensions to those who are totally disabled.
It is 25 years ago since I first spoke on behalf of the blind in this country. We have always been reluctant to consider their case. As the hon. member who has just taken his seat pointed out, the numbers involved are of no great political significance, and the amount of money involved is comparatively small. But the principle at stake is great. I cannot help thinking that the ages between
Blind Persons Act
16 and 20 are ages of uncertainty. They are the time when boys and girls encounter great difficulties, and begin to wonder where they are going and what the future holds for them. Those are the years when their minds are in some state of turmoil. Surely if we can reduce the eligible age from 21 to 18 years we could reduce it to 16 and give these young persons a break, these children whose education is always more difficult and more expensive, these children who many times must travel long distances to get their education, and must be accompanied in their travels.
Hon. members know, I am sure, that among the blind are to be found some of the most brilliant persons in this country. I know many of them who are more capable of earning their living than some hon. members of the House of Commons would be if they were deprived of their indemnities. We know there is a vast difference in the abilities of those who can see. There are only a few who are in class A and are outstanding. Those who are in darkness the whole 24 hours in the day must be brilliant indeed, when they can survive. They are proud persons, persons who perhaps would not have been so clever had they been able to see. They have been forced by circumstances to develop their talents to meet the obligations their handicap involves.
Even though they may be trained in new scientific methods to help them meet their handicap, it seems a pity that their whole living becomes more difficult. Their earning capacity is generally depreciated, and in order to fit themselves to meet their handicap they must begin early. In these days, when we are spending so much money, and when we are so boastful of our social services, I would urge that we spend more on behalf of these unfortunate persons. Sometimes I think we have gone a long way in establishing social services in our rich country; but when we have established those services for those who are physically fit we should not quibble, we should not be niggardly, we should not argue about the amount involved when the suggestion is made that the age limit be reduced from 18 to 16 years.
There are not many blind in Canada today in that age group. The hon. member for Lanark has said that only $2,500,000 would be involved. Surely very little more would be needed to include those of 16 years of age, so they would be given the break to which they are entitled. Those of us who can see and who have our other faculties have never been forced to discipline ourselves as they have. Perhaps because of our indolence we do not

Blind Persons Act
realize the great care that must be exercised by the parents of blind persons so they may be fitted for their tasks in life.
Surely we can reduce the age to 16 years. After all, family allowance payments end at 16, as do mothers' allowances. What is to become of the blind child whose mother is unwell; how is he to survive in those most critical years of his life? Because we know they are critical years, even for those who can see; and certainly they must be tragic for those who cannot.
At this time, when the minister is reducing the age to 18 years-and I join with the hon. member for Lanark and others who have complimented him upon that action-why should he not reduce it to 16? I doubt if even that is far enough. If the age limit were reduced to 16 it would help meet during two more years the handicap of these unfortunate people.
