speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is significant that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has remained on the sidelines for such a long time while this proposal has been debated in the committee.
I agree with the other hon. members who have spoken from this side of the house. The proposal is quite inadequate. When one considers our physical resources in Canada and the very small number of people involved in this legislation I feel sure we should go at least as far as the Canadian council of the blind and the Canadian National Institute for the Blind have suggested.
Other members have referred to the excellent material supplied to all hon. members by these two organizations. I do not propose to repeat any of the material that has been dealt with, but one paragraph has not been referred to. These organizations mentioned that in Canada we spend approximately $38 per month compared with $56 per month in the United States. When one considers that our resources on a per capita basis are very great I am sure that if we brought our contribution up in line with what is paid in the United States it would not place any great strain on us.
I realize it is not too difficult for hon. members on this side of the house to ask the government to increase its commitments for various projects, but when one considers the handicaps that this small handful of about 8,000 Canadian people face when they go through life unable to see, then this is a matter to which those of us who have the good fortune to have good health should give more consideration.
Many years ago when I was at university I realized what a handicap it is to go through 
life unable to see. A young chap came to Saskatoon to give a musical recital. He and his mother stayed with friends of mine. My friend telephoned and wondered whether I would take time to show this blind boy through the university. I of course was very glad to accept the invitation and we visited the gymnasium, the convocation hall and some of the lecture theatres. The president of the university was kind enough to shake hands with him and ask him some questions. Later that night around the dinner table the young blind chap told his mother and his hosts of what he saw at the university. Although I had been at the university for some time I would not have been able to tell a group of people in as great detail and with as much enthusiasm about the wonders of the University of Saskatchewan as this young lad who was unable to see was able to do. He never had been able to see, and would never be able to see.
When it is proposed, as the minister is now proposing, that we should make the pension available at 18, it should be explained to us why the Canadian economy will not stand the strain of commencing the pension at 16. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam pointed out, any child in Canada with the misfortune of being unable to see should have a pension available as soon as his sight is lost. We should regard our expenditures in this field as investments that will pay rich dividends to all the Canadian people. It has been one of our mistakes in the past that we have regarded payments of this sort as charity, as something we must do without very much enthusiasm.
The minister should be able to convince the rest of his colleagues that it is our responsibility to those who are blind to see that pensions be given without any means test. Since we are able to provide family allowances without any means test, and since everyone on reaching the age of 70 receives a pension without a means test, therefore it is not unreasonable that everyone who has the misfortune to be blind should have a pension without a means test. If there be those who do not require this money the Minister of National Revenue will be able to catch up with them eventually through the income tax machinery. It is a very fair device. If there are people who get the old age pension or family allowances and who can get by without them, the Minister of National Revenue is able to make some sort of adjustment with them.
Therefore the minister should give careful consideration to the suggestions that have come from this side of the house to the effect that pensions for the blind should be made

available without a means test. If he is unwilling to recommend that the pension start when blindness occurs, he should at least meet the representations that when family-allowances are discontinued the payment of pensions for blindness should commence. Since the minister has not committed himself up to this time I hope he will agree to recommend to the cabinet that the suggestions that have been made from this side of the house be given favourable consideration by his colleagues.

Perhaps it might be appropriate at this time to say a few brief words on this resolution. I should like to think- and I do think-that the observations made by the hon. member for Lanark, who is always so constructive in his approach to matters in this house, and those of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar represent the best mood of this house in the constructive observations which they have just made.
I am sure the committee will not mind my making this observation, that if one had to introduce a particular measure on the occasion of an anniversary event, this would be the measure. My colleague the Minister of National Revenue and I-I do not know whether he is aware of it-are approaching the end of the anniversary of that day ten years ago when we were both sworn in as ministers of the crown. Being somewhat of a sentimentalist I rather think it is a happy note that I should be able to introduce a motion of this kind on this particular anniversary, which I would want to share with my colleague the Minister of National Revenue.
As the hon. member for Lanark has said, this resolution is a further step in our effort to improve the conditions of our blind population. As the hon. member for Peterborough has said, that group does not want from this house or from any other group in our country any sympathy whatsoever. It is a group that is self-reliant. The work of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, of L'Associa-tion Canadienne-frangaise des aveugles et 1'Institut Nazareth de Montreal and the Montreal association for the blind confirms all that I have just said about the self-reliance and the initiative which the blind people of our country are prepared to take from time to time.
This is not the first amendment respecting the blind that has been introduced in this house during the past few years. The age, which is now being lowered from 21 to 18, was lowered from 40 to 21 in 1947. Those of us, Mr. Chairman, who are making this proposal to the house at this time had the responsibility of sitting on your right when that amendment was introduced.
Blind Persons Act
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned the desirability of rehabilitation for the blind, and I am sure the committee will generally echo what he has said in that regard. I do not know of anything that is more constructive to assist the blind than the work of rehabilitation. In addition to that, under the national health program the government is now financing the cost of four glaucoma clinics, one in Toronto, two in Montreal, and one in the city of Quebec.
Glaucoma is Canada's most serious eye problem. We have urged every province to follow the examples set by the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec. In the past month we have approved a federal grant for the establishment of a glaucoma clinic for the province of New Brunswick in Fredericton, and also under the national health program we have provided financial assistance to a number of eye research investigations being carried out by the department of ophthalmology of the University of Toronto.
In addition, we have undertaken in the past seven years a program of remedial surgery to restore vision to blind pensioners where there is some hope of success. I think this particular story is one of the happiest I could relate to the house. Over 60 per cent of the cases which have been given remedial surgery under the arrangements we have made with the provinces for the joint assumption of full costs of the operations have been successful; vision has been restored to the point where the pensioner could resume a more nearly normal life, and in 60 per cent of all cases where remedial surgery was attempted the pensioner had vision restored and was taken off the blind assistance roll altogether.
That represents the determination and the desire of the administration to do what it can, not only to provide pensions but also to do something in a constructive way to improve permanently, if it can, the disability of failure in eyesight.

The numbers are about 210, which is a very considerable proportion when we consider the total blind population of Canada, and I may say there is no limitation. Any blind persons now on these rolls and in receipt of this assistance can qualify for this kind of treatment, and the provincial governments in cases where agreements exist are prepared to arrange for the best of medical treatment in the effort to improve conditions.
Reference has been made to the six-point program of the C.N.I.B. I need not go into all the particulars of those six points except

Blind Persons Act
to say that all of them have been met by the government with the exception of two; and in those two cases, when we come to the bill we will see that a very considerable proportion of those remaining points have been constructively dealt with by the administration.
The second last point I should like to make is this. The hon. member for DUfferin-Simcoe, with his usual vigour, urged that the age should be reduced from 18 to 16. When the house passed the Disabled Persons Act it provided that a person benefiting under that act could qualify at the age of 18 years. At that time, as now, a blind person could qualify only at the age of 21 under the Blind Persons Act. The Blind Persons Act is disability legislation. It was the first legislation for disabled people in this country, and when from time to time I have met the various associations of the blind I have pointed out that improvements in the legislation which we had in mind for them would have to wait until such time as we could provide for the other classes of disabled persons for whom, up to that time, we had made no provision whatsoever.
I may say that the associations who came to see me were all agreed that we should do our best, first of all, to improve the lot of the other disabled classes of the country for whom no provision whatsoever had been made. What we are doing tonight with regard to the age qualification is to put the blind now on the same footing as that on which we have put the disabled persons.
Under the Disabled Persons Act the qualifying age is 18, and now through these present amendments we are making provision for the blind to be treated the same from the point of view of age as we treat the other disabled under the disability legislation; so I think, now that we have both these disabled groups in this particular on the same footing, whatever consideration is given at some later date can be dealt with on equal terms, now that we are face to face with the amendment before the house at the present time.
On this side, Mr. Chairman, with the support of the house we have in the last five and a half years lowered the age from 40 to 21; now under this legislation it is lowered to 18. We have abolished provisions removing from aliens, Indians, Eskimos and inmates of mental hospitals the disabilities which they suffered under the legislation before these amendments came into effect. We have abolished provincial residence requirements. We have abolished provisions for recovery from estates. We have abolished provisions which existed until 1947 by which married couples who were both blind received only half their

pensions. So in these and in countless other ways I think the administration has shown its concern and its desire to improve the welfare of the blind citizens of Canada.
There need be nothing else said on this occasion. When we reach the discussion stage of the bill we can go into some particulars already discussed, answer certain suggestions that have been made, and deal with the problem in a more specific way. But at this resolution stage I would want to join on behalf of the government with those who have taken part in the debate in noting the progress that has been made. Notwithstanding the criticism which may be levelled at what the government has done in this particular or in others, I think we may all say with conviction that every Canadian can feel proud that through this measure he is doing something to help those of his fellow citizens who bear the heavy handicap of blindness.
In time we can hope that medical science will prevent more people from losing their sight. We can be confident that new drugs and new skills will be developed to lead others back from the unending night of blindness; but those Canadians who are now without the faculty of sight and those who will lose it in the years ahead will continue, I know, to receive our admiration, our concern and our support. They can be sure of our unfailing and continuing help.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a brief word or two. First of all, I should like to congratulate the minister on the introduction of this legislation. It has already been stated that everybody is in agreement with it. I realize that at this time, in connection with the other legislation, it may not be possible to remove the means test entirely, but this is a step in the right direction. Perhaps a great many people in the country do not favour the removal of the means test in every phase of social security.
In this case I have had many resolutions sent to me from branches of the women's institute and various other organizations who favour the removal of the means test altogether. My own point of view is that when, some time in the future, financial conditions are such that the government feels able to remove the means test, the reason for doing so may very well be this. Since in this country equalization of opportunity is one of the principles on which the democratic way of life is based, and since the loss of a person's eyesight is the loss of one of his most valuable assets, a pension in a small way compensates a person for the loss of this

valuable physical asset and helps to make up for the opportunities he would otherwise have enjoyed.
There is one suggestion I should like to make for the consideration of the minister, and it is this. It is my understanding that, for the purposes of primary and, as it is sometimes called, secondary education the facilities now in existence are quite adequate for the blind. However, for those who are extremely ambitious and who have superior intelligence-and as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has pointed out, many persons who are blind have a high degree of intelligence and, because of their disability, have a great deal of ambition-some type of facility should be provided to enable them to have books printed in braille in order that they may advance to university education.
I realize that it would be impossible for universities all over the country to have these books, as they are extremely costly. I suggest for the minister's consideration that possibly the national library might be enabled to provide books giving advanced information in the arts and sciences and in technical fields, and that these books in braille might be sent out on loan to the universities. Or as an alternative-although I think this is a less meritorious suggestion-possibly one university could be designated as the recipient or holder of these books, and blind persons desirous of obtaining a university education could go to that university.
Those are just suggestions. I hope the minister will take them into consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I will take but a few minutes of the time of the house to make a few observations to the government regarding the resolution now before the house, and more particularly to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). Like all hon. members who have spoken before me, I wholeheartedly endorse this innovation and especially the resolution.
I will take the liberty-as I think this is a fitting occasion-of congratulating in a special way the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, which has played an important part in bringing considerable assistance to the unfortunate victims of, blindness.
Like those who have spoken before me, I would ask the government whether it would not be possible to lower the age of entitlement to the pension from 18 to 16 years, as requested a few moments ago.
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that between the ages of 16 and 18 is the time
Blind Persons Act
when a child is most in need of a pension, especially if he belongs to a large family. I might tell the minister that the constituency which I have the honour to represent is a working class constituency, with large families, several members of which are afflicted with this unfortunate disease.
May I therefore make the following suggestion? If to receive the family allowance a child has only to be born, or again if to receive the old age pension one has only to reach the age of 70, I fail to see why any blind person, of whatever age, could not receive the blind pension from the moment medical science declares that person to be blind. Even in the case of a child under 16 the blind pension could be paid immediately in lieu of the family allowance paid until then.
Mr. Chairman, I might perhaps be allowed to suggest something to the minister. Many are those-there are some in my riding and I would like in particular to submit one case to the minister-who are not truly blind in a medical sense. However, the weakness of their eyesight prevents them from being gainfully employed. Nobody wants to hire them. May I be permitted to refer to the case I just mentioned and point out to the minister that a young fellow in my riding, a member of the Association for the Blind and a recipient of their help, requested a pension but was found ineligible under the law as a blind person, his eyesight being better than the minimum by one or two tenths, so that he is no longer considered to be blind, no longer belongs to the association and is left without any help from them as well as from the government. He is therefore reduced to public beggary.
I urge the government, which has just made a step in the right direction, to take a close look at this act in order to see if it would not be possible to make medical exams not quite so strict, so that those who are blind but are not recognized as completely blind under the Blind Persons Act may get some assistance.
Once more I unreservedly congratulate the minister on the presentation of this resolution. It is indeed a great step in the right direction, and I hope that the suggestions which have been made by some members of the opposition will enable the minister to draft the bill so as to bring another measure of relief to those whom Providence has not favoured in that respect.

After a person has been in Canada for five years he becomes a Canadian citizen if he has fulfilled all other qualifications, and I believe that would be the proper time at which to extend to that person the same rights and privileges that are extended to any other person in Canada.
I make a plea to the minister to consider the reduction of the residence qualification from ten years to five. There are many supporting arguments I could use in so urging, but I do not think it is necessary for me to do so. The minister is quite aware of the problem, and I can only hope he will give some consideration to the question before the bill is introduced in the house.
